title: Timing of Earliest Documented Positive Hepatitis C Laboratory Result Relative to Delivery Among Pregnant Persons With Active Infection in West Virginia, 2022-2023.
abstract: Direct-acting antiviral therapy can cure hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection; however, because treatment is not recommended during pregnancy, preconception treatment remains the primary strategy to prevent perinatal HCV exposure. West Virginia birth records from 2022 to 2023 were linked with statewide HCV laboratory surveillance data. This linked dataset was used to identify births to persons with active HCV infection and characterize the timing of the earliest documented positive HCV laboratory result relative to delivery. A total of 426 deliveries resulting in 433 HCV-exposed live-born infants were identified. Most pregnant persons were aged 25-34 years, White and insured by Medicaid. Overall, 38.5% had their earliest documented positive HCV laboratory result more than 5 years prior to delivery, 36.9% had their first documented positive test 1-5 years prior to delivery and 24.6% had their first documented positive test within 1 year before delivery and up to 2 weeks postpartum. These findings indicate that many pregnant persons with active HCV infection had documented longstanding infection prior to pregnancy, highlighting opportunities to strengthen linkage to care and access to curative treatment before pregnancy.

title: Microbial Oncology: A Critical Appraisal of Microbe-associated Carcinogenesis from Established Infectious Causes to the Contested Tumour Microbiome
abstract: Infectious agents remain among the few modifiable causes of human cancer for which prevention has already altered population-level incidence, yet the intellectual boundaries of the field have shifted substantially. Classical infectious carcinogenesis, built on a small set of viruses, bacteria and parasites with documented aetiological roles, now coexists with a far broader proposition that resident microbial communities within tumours and at distant mucosal sites shape tumour initiation, progression and treatment response. This review examines how securely that broader proposition is supported, and where the evidence remains provisional. Literature was identified through structured searching of biomedical and multidisciplinary scholarly sources, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and by targeted retrieval of corrections and retractions, with appraisal focused on study design, biological specificity, contamination control, replication and the distance between mechanistic plausibility and demonstrated clinical effect. Several conclusions are well supported: oncogenic viruses operate largely through sustained expression of viral oncoproteins and genomic integration; Helicobacter pylori eradication reduces gastric cancer incidence, although the absolute benefit depends strongly on baseline risk and mucosal stage at treatment; and vaccination against hepatitis B virus and human papillomavirus has produced measurable declines in attributable malignancy. Evidence for bacterial contributions to colorectal carcinogenesis is mechanistically rich but complicated by unresolved taxonomy, inconsistent detection thresholds and limited prospective data. The pan-cancer intratumoural microbiome literature has been materially destabilised by demonstrated analytical errors and a high-profile retraction, which narrowed rather than abolished the field's claims. Microbiota-based prediction of immunotherapy response replicates only partially across cohorts, and randomised faecal microbiota transplantation evidence remains small and early phase. The central unresolved problems concern causal attribution in low-biomass settings, strain-level rather than genus-level resolution, and the near-absence of prospective interventional designs capable of distinguishing microbial drivers from microbial consequences of established tumours. Progress will depend less on additional descriptive surveys than on contamination-controlled, strain-resolved and prospectively designed studies.

title: Direct-Acting Antiviral Therapy in Patients With Hepatocellular Carcinoma Receiving Non-Curative Treatment: High Sustained Virological Response Rates and Preservation of Liver Functional Reserve.
abstract: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) cure most chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections, but their impact on liver functional reserve in patients with a history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly after non-curative HCC treatment, remains unclear. We evaluated antiviral efficacy and liver functional reserve after DAA therapy according to HCC history and timing of DAA initiation. In this retrospective single-center cohort, 716 patients initiated DAA therapy, and 690 with evaluable sustained virological response at 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12) were analysed. Patients were classified as no HCC, curative-treated HCC, or non-curative-treated HCC according to the most recent HCC treatment before DAA initiation. Liver functional reserve was assessed using the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score, modified ALBI grade, and Child-Pugh class. In the non-curative-treated HCC group, early (≤ 3 months) versus delayed (> 3 months) DAA initiation after the most recent HCC treatment was compared. Overall SVR12 was 96.1%, with similarly high rates across groups regardless of HCC history. The median ALBI score improved from -2.35 to -2.58 at SVR12 in the curative-treated HCC group (p < 0.001) but remained unchanged in the non-curative-treated HCC group (-2.36 to -2.38). Among 64 patients with a history of HCC, 43 (67.2%) developed recurrence; in these patients, the ALBI score improved from -2.31 at DAA initiation to -2.57 at recurrence (p < 0.001), and more than 90% remained Child-Pugh class A. Early and delayed DAA initiation showed similarly high SVR12 rates and comparable liver functional reserve. DAAs achieved high SVR12 rates and maintained liver functional reserve in patients with HCV, including those with a history of HCC after non-curative treatment.

In this retrospective single-center cohort, 716 patients initiated DAA therapy, and 690 with evaluable sustained virological response at 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12) were analysed. Patients were classified as no HCC, curative-treated HCC, or non-curative-treated HCC according to the most recent HCC treatment before DAA initiation. Liver functional reserve was assessed using the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score, modified ALBI grade, and Child-Pugh class. In the non-curative-treated HCC group, early (≤ 3 months) versus delayed (> 3 months) DAA initiation after the most recent HCC treatment was compared. Overall SVR12 was 96.1%, with similarly high rates across groups regardless of HCC history. The median ALBI score improved from -2.35 to -2.58 at SVR12 in the curative-treated HCC group (p < 0.001) but remained unchanged in the non-curative-treated HCC group (-2.36 to -2.38). Among 64 patients with a history of HCC, 43 (67.2%) developed recurrence; in these patients, the ALBI score improved from -2.31 at DAA initiation to -2.57 at recurrence (p < 0.001), and more than 90% remained Child-Pugh class A. Early and delayed DAA initiation showed similarly high SVR12 rates and comparable liver functional reserve. DAAs achieved high SVR12 rates and maintained liver functional reserve in patients with HCV, including those with a history of HCC after non-curative treatment.

title: Butyrate ameliorates acute‐on‐chronic liver failure by regulating macrophage polarization
abstract: ABSTRACT Gut microbiota dysbiosis and its metabolite disorders may drive the progression of hepatitis B virus‐related acute‐on‐chronic liver failure (HBV‐ACLF) through the gut–liver axis, but the specific mechanisms and intervention targets remain unclear. Blood and stool samples were collected from 50 patients with liver disease at different stages and subjected to metagenomic, metabolomic, and transcriptomic sequencing to elucidate the microbiota–metabolism–immune characteristics of HBV‐ACLF. We evaluated changes in gut microbiota composition, short‐chain fatty acids, intestinal barrier integrity, liver injury, and immune cell function following fecal microbiota transplantation or butyrate supplementation, and explored specific regulatory mechanisms in ACLF mouse models and RAW264.7 cells. HBV‐ACLF was associated with loss of beneficial gut microbes, reduced butyrate, a weakened intestinal barrier, and increased leakage of bacterial components into the bloodstream, which further exacerbated liver inflammation. Butyrate strengthened the intestinal barrier, reduced lipopolysaccharide leakage, and suppressed M1 macrophage polarization, further improving ACLF disease progression. Mechanistic analysis revealed that butyrate inhibited the phosphorylation of the mitogen‐activated protein kinase signaling pathway within macrophages, thereby suppressing their polarization towards the pro‐inflammatory M1 phenotype. These findings support a chain linking gut microbes, short‐chain fatty acids, and immune dysregulation in ACLF, and highlight butyrate‐based modulation as a potential therapeutic strategy for ACLF.

title: PO157 | DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGES IN PREGNANCY-TRIGGERED IMMUNE-MEDIATED THROMBOTIC THROMBOCYTOPENIC PURPURA: A CASE FOR EARLY AND ACCURATE IDENTIFICATION
abstract: Immune-mediated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (iTTP) is a rare and potentially fatal thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) characterized by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency due to the presence of inhibitory autoantibodies. iTTP typically presents with the classic pentad of thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, neurological symptoms, renal dysfunction, and fever. However, the clinical presentation can overlap with other pregnancy-related TMAs, such as subset of HELLP syndrome and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), complicating timely diagnosis. Pregnancy is a known trigger for iTTP, and rapid recognition is crucial to avoid maternal and fetal complications. The PLASMIC score has been validated as an effective tool for early risk stratification, facilitating prompt therapeutic intervention. Early diagnosis and treatment with plasma exchange, immunosuppressive agents, and novel therapies such as caplacizumab are critical for improving outcomes in this life-threatening condition.Patients and Methods. A 28-year-old woman at 32 weeks of gestation presented with abdominal pain, severe asthenia and acute neurological symptoms. Laboratory evaluation revealed severe microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia with hemoglobin 5.1 g/dL (reference range [RR] 12–16), platelet count 40 ×103/mm3 (RR 150–400), markedly elevated lactate dehydrogenase 2279 U/L (RR 135–250), reticulocytosis 330.9 ×103/μL (RR 22.0–139.0), indirect hyperbilirubinemia 0.99 mg/dL (RR 0.1–0.9) and undetectable haptoglobin, in the absence of coagulopathy and with mild renal impairment. Due to maternal-fetal deterioration, emergency cesarean section was performed. Peripheral blood smear demonstrated 3% schistocytes. Early clinical probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency was assessed using the PLASMIC score. A comprehensive diagnostic work-up excluded secondary TMAs, including autoimmune disorders (ANA, ENA, antiphospholipid antibodies, ANCA, lupus anticoagulant), infections (CMV, EBV, HBV, HCV, HIV, TORCH), malignancy, immune hemolysis (Coombs tests) and active infections (negative microbiological cultures).Results. The PLASMIC score was 6, indicating high risk of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. ADAMTS13 activity was undetectable (0%) with detectable inhibitory anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, confirming iTTP. Immediate treatment with therapeutic plasma exchange, high-dose corticosteroids and caplacizumab resulted in rapid neurological recovery and platelet count normalization. Persistently suppressed ADAMTS13 activity prompted early anti-CD20 therapy with rituximab, achieving progressive enzymatic recovery. The patient was discharged in stable condition and scheduled for close hematologic monitoring.Conclusions. This case underscores the importance of rapid hematologic assessment and early risk stratification in pregnancy-associated TMAs. Integration of PLASMIC score–guided decision-making with prompt initiation of plasma exchange, caplacizumab and immunosuppressive therapy represents the current standard of care for iTTP and is feasible and effective even in the peripartum setting.

title: The National Immunisation Programme in the Netherlands. Surveillance and developments in 2025-2026
abstract: Het RIVM houdt elk jaar bij hoeveel mensen een ziekte krijgen waartegen het Rijksvaccinatieprogramma (RVP) vaccineert. In 2025 kregen minder mensen bof (150), kinkhoest (333), ernstige pneumokokkenziekte (1.941) of een infectie door het rotavirus dan in de jaren ervoor. De aantallen voor difterie (7), acute hepatitis B (100), meningokokkenziekte (137) en tetanus (3) waren ongeveer hetzelfde als in eerdere jaren. Net als in de afgelopen jaren kwamen rodehond en polio niet voor. Meer mensen werden ziek van Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib, 73) dan de afgelopen drie jaar. Opvallend was het aantal mensen met mazelen (539). Dat waren er veel meer dan in 2023-2024 en het waren vooral kinderen die niet zijn gevaccineerd. Eén volwassene is aan mazelen overleden. In 2025 zijn meer dan 1 miljoen kinderen tot 18 jaar gevaccineerd binnen het RVP. Zij kregen samen meer dan 2,4 miljoen vaccinaties. Ook zijn meer dan 100.000 zwangeren gevaccineerd tegen griep en/of kinkhoest. In totaal kregen zij meer dan 130.000 vaccinaties. Deze vaccinaties beschermen hun baby in de eerste maanden na de geboorte tegen deze ziekten. In 2025 en 2026 zijn een aantal zaken veranderd in het RVP. Sinds de herfst van 2025 krijgen baby's in hun eerste levensjaar een prik tegen het RS-virus. Dit virus kan bij jonge kinderen ernstige infecties aan de luchtwegen veroorzaken. In de winter van 2025-2026 kwamen veel minder baby's met dit virus op de intensive care terecht. Ook zijn de momenten waarop kinderen de vaccinaties krijgen (het vaccinatieschema) aangepast om hen nog beter te beschermen. Kinderen krijgen bijvoorbeeld hun tweede vaccinatie tegen bof, mazelen en rodehond (BMR) nu als ze drie jaar zijn in plaats van negen jaar. Verder wordt een nieuw pneumokokkenvaccin gebruikt dat tegen meer typen beschermt.

title: An Atlas of Antiviral Therapeutic Outcomes: How Viral Biology Shapes the Reach of Treatment
abstract: Antiviral inhibition does not produce a single therapeutic endpoint: some infections can be cured after finite treatment, others require durable suppression, and others remain difficult to influence because the actionable phase is brief or anatomically inaccessible. These different outcomes reflect the biological state that preserves infection or permits return, the time during which a drug-sensitive process remains causally important, the anatomical space in which consequential virus or viral material resides, and the capacity of viral populations to evolve under therapeutic pressure. Here, we examine these relationships across curable, suppressible, latent, acute, neuroinvasive, and post-acute viral infections. Comparisons among HCV, HIV-1, HBV, HSV, influenza, RSV, dengue, SARS-CoV-2, Ebola virus, CHIKV, and other systems show how persistence architecture, diagnostic timing, tissue pharmacology, host context, and resistance can determine whether antiviral activity translates into virological cure, durable suppression, recurrence control, prevention, or incomplete therapeutic control. Human challenge studies, clinical programs with discordant outcomes, and resistance studies further illustrate where mechanistic activity and therapeutic sufficiency diverge. Across these examples, antiviral outcome depends ultimately on whether treatment can intercept the biological state that determines the subsequent fate of infection.

Human challenge studies, clinical programs with discordant outcomes, and resistance studies further illustrate where mechanistic activity and therapeutic sufficiency diverge. Across these examples, antiviral outcome depends ultimately on whether treatment can intercept the biological state that determines the subsequent fate of infection.

title: Recommendations to Enhance Engagement in Perinatal Research With People Who Inject Drugs.
abstract: Women of reproductive age are significantly less likely than men to initiate hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, with the lowest uptake among women with children. Women who inject drugs who have children are a highly marginalised and stigmatised population who experience inequitable access to healthcare and poorer health outcomes. In the BUMP-C qualitative study-Bridging Unified Management of Pregnancy in hepatitis C care-we sought to investigate current HCV care pathways and perceptions of HCV management during pregnancy among women who inject drugs. During this study, several lessons emerged from both the challenges and successes in engaging with this population. The aim of this commentary is to outline key recommendations for optimally engaging women who inject drugs in perinatal research. These recommendations include building trust with research participants, promoting strategies for research flexibility and seeking and valuing community and lived experience. The voices of women who inject drugs, often neglected in this space, must be prioritised to improve health outcomes for them and their children.

title: Knowledge, Preventive Practices, and Risk Behaviors Related to Sexually Transmitted Infections Among Adolescent and Young Adult Students at a Faculty of Dentistry in Costa Rica
abstract: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are a major global public health concern, particularly among young people. Dentists play a key role in the early detection of STIs, given their oral manifestations; however, gaps persist between STI knowledge and preventive behaviors among young people, including dental students. To assess knowledge and risk behaviors related to STIs dental students aged 18-25 years at a university in Costa Rica. A cross-sectional, email-based survey was administered to students aged 18-25 years between May and July 2025. The questionnaire covered sociodemographic characteristics, sexual behaviors, STI knowledge, preventive practices, and sources of information. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used, with a significance level of p<0.05. A total of 294 students participated, the majority of whom were women and early-year students; 74.2% reported sexual activity. Overall STI knowledge was predominantly moderate, while prevention knowledge was high. Gaps were identified regarding bacterial STIs and hepatitis B transmission. Age, academic year, and history of sexual activity were significantly associated with higher knowledge levels. Among sexually active participants, consistent condom use during vaginal intercourse was 61.1% but was substantially lower for oral sex (4.7%). Only 38.9% undergone STI testing, and 3.5% reported a previous STI diagnosis. A weak positive correlation was found between STI knowledge and STI prevention knowledge (rs=0.21, p=0.001). Although dental students demonstrate moderate STI knowledge, gaps and risk behaviors persist, particularly regarding oral transmission and prevention, highlighting the need to enhance comprehensive sexual health education.

title: A review on prevalence, clinical features, and risk factors of hepatitis A virus infection in Sri Lanka
abstract: Hepatitis A virus (HAV), which causes hepatitis A, remains a global public health concern. HAV is transmitted primarily through the faeco-oral route, either by ingestion of contaminated food or water or through direct person-to-person contact. HAV causes acute viral hepatitis but does not lead to chronic infection. This review examined locally published literature on the prevalence, clinical features, and risk factors of HAV infection in Sri Lanka. A literature search was conducted on publicly accessible PubMed, SLJOL and DOAJ databases on 1st June 2025 using a keyword search [hepatitis A] OR [type A hepatitis] AND [Sri Lanka]. The search yielded 46 publications, of which nine research articles were included in the present review. The findings showed that the sero-prevalence of HAV infections in Sri Lanka ranged from 10.8% to 88.8%. Sri Lanka shows a widespread exposure to HAV, with differences in sero-prevalence across geographical areas and study cohorts. The reported clinical features were comparable to those described in the global literature. Risk factors for acquiring HAV infection included poor knowledge of hepatitis A, poor hygiene, unsafe drinking water, low income, and urban residence.

title: Sexual and reproductive health of women living on illegal gold mining sites in French Guiana: a multicentric cross-sectional survey
abstract: Background Women involved in illegal gold mining in French Guiana face intersecting vulnerabilities related to migration, informality, and precarious living and working conditions, which heighten their exposure to sexual and gender-based violence and undermine sexual and reproductive health. However, quantitative data on these issues in this population remain scarce. This study aimed to document the sexual and reproductive health of these marginalized women. Methods A cross-sectional descriptive survey was conducted among women involved in illegal gold mining. Participants were recruited at logistical bases at the borders with Suriname and Brazil. After providing informed consent, participants were interviewed by trained field investigators using a standardized questionnaire. It collected information on sociodemographic characteristics, exposure to sexual and gender-based violence, engagement in transactional sex, obstetrical history, access to gynecological care, and testing for sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistical methods. Results Among the 115 women included, 14.0% reported sexual assault or rape (95% CI: 8.2–21.8), and 19.1% reported intimate partner violence. Regarding transactional sex, 9.5% of women were currently engaged in sex work, and 8.7% reported past involvement, among whom 80.9% reported systematic condom use. Overall, 15.6% of women reported a history of induced abortion (95% CI: 9.5–23.6), and half were performed by a healthcare provider. Most participants (80.0%) reported up-to-date gynecological follow-up (95% CI: 71.5–86.8). Previous HIV testing was relatively common (65.2%), whereas testing for hepatitis B (33.9%), hepatitis C (28.7%), and syphilis (35.6%) were less frequent. Conclusions Women working in mining areas faced high levels of sexual and intimate partner violence, while transactional sex appeared less aligned with commonly held stereotypes. Despite relatively good access to gynecological care, abortion rates remained high and STIs screening coverage could be improved. Promoting systematic screening for gender-based violence within sexual and reproductive health services is essential. Clinical Trial Registration: NCT05540470.

title: Real-world outcomes of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma: A retrospective cohort study
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) ranks sixth in morbidity and third in mortality among oncological diseases in the world. The combination of atezolizumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor) and bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) is the standard of first-line systemic therapy for unresectable HCC based on the results of the randomized IMbrave150 trial. Data on the use of this scheme in real clinical practice in the Russian population remains limited. To assess the efficacy and safety of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in HCC patients in a real-world single-center setting. Materials and methods. This retrospective cohort study included 15 patients with histologically or clinically confirmed HCC receiving atezolizumab 1200 mg + bevacizumab 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks at Medical Center Medical City (Tyumen) from 2021 to 2025. The median age of the patients included in the study was 49.6 years (range 27.6–73.1 years; mean 51.9 ± 12.3 years). Male patients prevailed – 10 (66.7%), 5 (33.3%) women. Stage BCLC C – 66.7% (10/15), BCLC B – 5/15 (33.3%). Viral hepatitis C was detected in 46.7% (7/15) of patients, hepatitis B in 13.3% (2/15), and the viral etiology of HCC was not established in 40.0% (6/15) of patients. The medians of PFS and OS were not reached, and the median follow-up was 16 months. The average number of courses conducted is 9 (range 2–21). Adverse events were reported in 26.7% (4/15) of patients; the most significant were grade 1–2 autoimmune hepatitis, thrombocytopenia, and ischemic stroke. Real-world data confirm the efficacy and manageable toxicity of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in HCC.

title: CO026 | LIVER FIBROSIS, STEATOSIS, AND SUBCLINICAL ATHEROSCLEROSIS IN PATIENTS WITH HEMOPHILIA: A CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY
abstract: Background and Aims. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasingly recognized as a driver of cardiovascular risk beyond traditional factors. At the same time, patients with hemophilia (PWH) are aging and accumulating metabolic comorbidities such as obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia and are therefore no longer protected from arterial disease. However, liver involvement in this population is heterogeneous and often reflects a complex interplay between metabolic dysfunction and previous viral infections. As a result, it remains unclear whether liver fibrosis and steatosis truly identify patients at increased cardiovascular risk in hemophilia. This study aimed to explore the relationship between liver fibrosis, steatosis, and subclinical atherosclerosis in a cohort of PWH. We report an interim analysis of a cross-sectional study evaluating liver health in PWH. Liver fibrosis was assessed and graded from F0 to F4, while liver steatosis was evaluated and graded from S0 to S3. Subclinical atherosclerosis was assessed and recorded as present or absent. Clinical data included age, hemophilia type and severity, viral history (HCV, HBV, HIV), liver enzymes, platelet count, FIB-4, and traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Fibrosis and steatosis were analyzed as both ordinal variables and clinically relevant categories. Associations with atherosclerosis were assessed using non-parametric tests and contingency-table analyses. A total of 49 patients with hemophilia were included (median age 55 years). Baseline characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1. Subclinical atherosclerosis was detected in 8/45 patients (16.3%). Liver fibrosis was generally mild, with significant fibrosis (F2–F4) observed in 6/49 patients (12.2%). Steatosis was present in 21/41 patients (51.2%), with moderate-to-severe steatosis (S2–S3) in 11/41 (26.8%). No significant association was found between fibrosis stage and the presence of atherosclerosis (p=0.524). Similarly, steatosis was not associated with atherosclerosis (p=0.389). Traditional cardiovascular risk factors were common, with hypertension in 42.8%, dyslipidemia in 32.6%, and active or previous smoking in 71.4% of patients. source_records.abstract: Background and Aims. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is increasingly recognized as a driver of cardiovascular risk beyond traditional factors. At the same time, patients with hemophilia (PWH) are aging and accumulating metabolic comorbidities such as obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia and are therefore no longer protected from arterial disease. However, liver involvement in this population is heterogeneous and often reflects a complex interplay between metabolic dysfunction and previous viral infections. As a result, it remains unclear whether liver fibrosis and steatosis truly identify patients at increased cardiovascular risk in hemophilia. title: Exploring NS5A Protein of Hepatitis C Virus Through Computational Deep Learning Models and Phylogenetic Analysis for Sequence Variability
abstract: Background: Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) remains a global health threat, causing severe liver diseases such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Protein sequences are essential for exploring genetic variability and improving detection. This study presents a generative LSTM model, AI-VNA, for generating and analyzing NS5A protein sequences to enhance understanding of sequence diversity and improve predictive modeling. Methods: The AI-VNA model was trained on curated NS5A protein sequences and evaluated against baseline models including CNN, 1D-CNN, GRU, and Simple RNN. Generated sequences were validated using BLAST (version 2.16.0) to assess biological relevance. Additional analyses included a sequence similarity heatmap, phylogenetic clustering using UPGMA, and statistical comparison of sequence similarities via the Mann–Whitney U test. Results: AI-VNA achieved 98.56% accuracy, outperforming other models and demonstrating strong capability in modeling sequence patterns. BLAST validation showed an average query coverage of 82%, an average E-value of 1 × 10−155, and 96.68% identity to known NS5A proteins. The sequence similarity heatmap revealed notable variability among the generated sequences. Phylogenetic analysis showed distinct clustering patterns, indicating both conservation and diversity. A box plot comparing similarity scores of predicted and database sequences showed significant variation (p = 0.01221; Cliff’s Delta = 0.291, small effect). Conclusions: These findings highlight the AI-VNA model’s ability to generate evolutionarily relevant and diverse NS5A protein sequences, supporting its potential for improving HCV sequence analysis and aiding in diagnostic and therapeutic developments.

title: Despite High Hepatitis C Virus Testing, Treatment Gaps Remain: A Study Among Syringe Services Program Participants in Massachusetts.
abstract: Background People who inject drugs are less likely to initiate hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, and less likely to achieve sustained virologic response if they do start, than the general population. The objective of this analysis was to examine whether healthcare experiences were associated with HCV testing and treatment outcomes among people who inject drugs in Massachusetts. Methods We analyzed baseline data from an HIV prevention study, which enrolled participants from two Massachusetts syringe service programs from 2020 to 2025. We assessed lifetime HCV testing and treatment outcomes, sociodemographics, substance use behaviors, and healthcare experiences (e.g., comfort with providers) and calculated bivariate associations. Results Among 185 participants (median age of 40, 43% cisgender women), 97% had ever been tested for HCV; 71% of those tested had ever received a positive test result. However, among those who tested positive, only 41% initiated treatment. Most participants reported comfort discussing their injection drug use with a provider (79%) and feeling welcome in medical clinics (75%). Cisgender men and those feeling welcome in medical clinics reported higher proportions of treatment initiation compared to their counterparts (both p Conclusions Despite pervasive testing and high treatment completion rates, treatment initiation remains suboptimal. Feeling welcome in medical clinics may be an important, modifiable indicator of HCV treatment engagement. The gap between HCV testing and treatment initiation persists. Understanding factors that shape HCV testing and treatment engagement can generate actionable insights for ongoing elimination efforts in New England.

full_text: Abstract Background Hepatitis B virus infection among pregnant women is a significant public health problem in Ethiopia. Although primary studies on HBV infection among pregnant women have been conducted across different regions in Ethiopia, a synthesized pooled estimate and associated factors remain fragmented. Therefore, this systematic review was aimed at summarising the available information and making an accurate estimate of hepatitis B virus infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. Different databases (Google Scholar, PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and African Journal Online) were searched to identify relevant studies published between January 1, 2021, and December 25, 2025 in Ethiopia. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used to assess the methodological qualities of the included studies. The random effect DerSimonian-Liard model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of Hepatitis B virus infection. I2 assessed the amount of heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test and a funnel plot. Results We included 25 studies conducted in Ethiopia. The pooled prevalence of hepatitis B infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia was 7.3% (95% CI: 6.3–8.4%), with significant heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 76.25%, p < 0.001). History of abortion(AOR = 3.81, 95%CI: 1.69–8.57), Body tattooing(AOR = 3.54, 95%CI: 1.65–7.58), Contact history with HBV patients(AOR = 8.38, 95%CI: 3.89,-18.06), HIV positivity(AOR = 10.04, 95%CI: 3.91–25.75), dental procedure(AOR = 3.64, 95%CI: 1.92, 6.92), Family history of HBV(AOR = 6.37, 95%CI: 3.83–10.6), History of blood transfusion(AOR = 6.32, 95%CI: 4.11–9.74), History of hospitalization(AOR = 3.99, 95%CI: 2.47–6.45), Multiple sexual partner(AOR = 7.91, 95%CI: 5.31–11.8) and Traditional tonsillectomy(AOR = 3.81, 95%CI: 1.92–7.57) were associated factors for hepatitis B infection among pregnant women. Conclusion A higher intermediate level of hepatitis B virus infection (2–7.99%) was observed among pregnant women in Ethiopia. Therefore, early detection of pregnant women, awareness creation on the mode of transmission of HBV, and early implementation of evidence-based control measures are recommended. analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, and publication bias was evaluated using Egger’s test and a funnel plot.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled prevalence of hepatitis B infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia was estimated at 7.3% (95% CI: 6.3–8.4%), with significant heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 76.25%, p < 0.001). analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that the available studies on HBV infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia are fragmented, and there is no consensus on the pooled estimate of prevalence. The significant heterogeneity (I2 = 76.25%) suggests variability in study designs and populations, which may affect the reliability of the pooled estimate. Additionally, the review notes that the evidence is limited in certain areas, such as the geographic distribution of risk factors and the impact of specific interventions.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Early detection of HBV infection in pregnant women, awareness creation on the mode of transmission, and the implementation of evidence-based control measures are recommended. Further research is needed to address the evidence gaps, particularly in understanding the mechanisms of transmission and the effectiveness of interventions in reducing HBV prevalence among pregnant women.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the prevalence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia and identify associated factors. A total of 25 studies published between 2021 and 2025 were included, and the pooled prevalence was found to be 7.3% (95% CI: 6.3–8.4%) with significant heterogeneity (I2 = 76.25%, p < 0.001). Several risk factors were identified, including history of abortion, body tattooing, contact with HBV patients, HIV positivity, dental procedures, family history of HBV, blood transfusion, hospitalization, multiple sexual partners, and traditional tonsillectomy. The review highlights the fragmented nature of the evidence and the need for more comprehensive studies to address the heterogeneity and gaps in understanding. The Joanna Briggs Institute tool was used to assess methodological quality, and the random effect DerSimonian-Liard model was applied to estimate pooled prevalence. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2, and publication bias was evaluated using Egger’s test and a funnel plot.
elements_en.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The pooled prevalence of hepatitis B infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia was estimated at 7.3% (95% CI: 6.3–8.4%), with significant heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 76.25%, p < 0.001). Several factors were identified as being associated with HBV infection, including history of abortion, body tattooing, contact history with HBV patients, HIV positivity, dental procedures, family history of HBV, history of blood transfusion, history of hospitalization, multiple sexual partners, and traditional tonsillectomy.
elements_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that the available studies on HBV infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia are fragmented, and there is no consensus on the pooled estimate of prevalence. The significant heterogeneity (I2 = 76.25%) suggests variability in study designs and populations, which may affect the reliability of the pooled estimate. Additionally, the review notes that the evidence is limited in certain areas, such as the geographic distribution of risk factors and the impact of specific interventions.
elements_en.research_and_practice_implications: Early detection of HBV infection in pregnant women, awareness creation on the mode of transmission, and the implementation of evidence-based control measures are recommended. Further research is needed to address the evidence gaps, particularly in understanding the mechanisms of transmission and the effectiveness of interventions in reducing HBV prevalence among pregnant women.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述旨在整合现有信息,对埃塞俄比亚孕妇中乙型肝炎病毒感染情况进行准确估计,并重点关注患病率及其相关因素。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 根据PRISMA 2020指南进行了系统综述和元分析。研究从多个数据库中识别,包括Google Scholar、PubMed、Embase、Web of Science、Scopus、Cochrane Library和African Journal Online,涵盖2021年1月1日至2025年12月25日的出版物。使用Joanna Briggs Institute工具评估方法学质量,并采用随机效应DerSimonian-Liard模型估计合并的患病率。使用I2评估异质性,并通过Egger’s检验和漏斗图评估发表偏倚。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 埃塞俄比亚孕妇中乙型肝炎病毒感染的汇总患病率估计为7.3%(95% CI:6.3–8.4%),研究间存在显著异质性(I2 = 76.25%,p < 0.001)。已确定多个与HBV感染相关的因素,包括流产史、身体纹身、与HBV患者接触史、HIV阳性、牙科治疗、HBV家族史、输血史、住院史、多个性伴侣以及传统扁桃体切除术。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 该综述指出,目前关于埃塞俄比亚孕妇乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)感染的研究是零散的,且对患病率的汇总估计值尚无共识。显著的异质性(I2 = 76.25%)表明研究设计和人群存在差异,这可能影响汇总估计值的可靠性。此外,综述还指出某些方面的证据有限,例如风险因素的地理分布以及特定干预措施的影响。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 建议早期检测孕妇中的HBV感染,提高对传播传播方式的认识,并实施基于证据的控制措施。需要进一步研究以解决证据缺口,特别是理解传播的机制以及干预措施在降低孕妇中HBV 患病率方面的有效性。

title_zh: 埃塞俄比亚孕妇中流行病学感染的乙型肝炎病毒:2021年至2025年发表数据的系统综述和荟萃分析
source_body_en: Therefore, this systematic review was aimed at summarising the available information and making an accurate estimate of hepatitis B virus infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. Results We included 25 studies conducted in Ethiopia. Conclusion A higher intermediate level of hepatitis B virus infection (2–7.99%) was observed among pregnant women in Ethiopia. Epidemiology of hepatitis B virus infection among pregnant women in Ethiopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of data published between 2021 and 2025. History of abortion(AOR = 3.81, 95%CI: 1.69–8.57), Body tattooing(AOR = 3.54, 95%CI: 1.65–7.58), Contact history with HBV patients(AOR = 8.38, 95%CI: 3.89,-18.06), HIV positivity(AOR = 10.04, 95%CI: 3.91–25.75), dental procedure(AOR = 3.64, 95%CI: 1.92, 6.92), Family history of HBV(AOR = 6.37, 95%CI: 3.83–10.6), History of blood transfusion(AOR = 6.32, 95%CI: 4.11–9.74), History of hospitalization(AOR = 3.99, 95%CI: 2.47–6.45), Multiple sexual partner(AOR = 7.91, 95%CI: 5.31–11.8) and Traditional tonsillectomy(AOR = 3.81, 95%CI: 1.92–7.57) were associated factors for hepatitis B infection among pregnant women. Abstract Background Hepatitis B virus infection among pregnant women is a significant public health problem in Ethiopia. Although primary studies on HBV infection among pregnant women have been conducted across different regions in Ethiopia, a synthesized pooled estimate and associated factors remain fragmented. full_text: ABSTRACTBackgroundHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain major public health challenges globally and in Ethiopia. Although policies, regulations, and strategies have been developed to support their control and elimination, translating these policy commitments into effective implementation remains challenging. Understanding stakeholder experiences and perspectives is important for identifying gaps in policy awareness, participation, implementation, and program coordination.ObjectiveThis study aimed to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia.MethodsA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted among stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, research, and service delivery. Thirty‐four participants were purposively selected based on their professional roles, experience, knowledge, and involvement in relevant programs. Data were collected from April 17 to May 27, 2023, using qualitative interviews and focus group discussions, complemented by a review of relevant policy, strategy, guideline, and program documents and observations of selected service‐delivery and pharmaceutical settings. Data were transcribed, translated where necessary, and thematically analysed using MAXQDA Analytics Pro 2024. The analysis focused on policy awareness, stakeholder involvement, stakeholder roles, implementation status, opportunities, and challenges.ResultsParticipants had a mean work experience of 16.82 years (SD = 0.79), and 30 (88.2%) were male. Of the 34 participants, 12 (35.3%) clearly identified or described the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies, while 22 (64.7%) did not. Fifteen (44.1%) participants reported stakeholder involvement in policy and strategy development, whereas 19 (55.9%) did not report adequate opportunities for participation. Most participants, 32 (94.1%), demonstrated an understanding of stakeholder roles and responsibilities in policy development and implementation. However, only 8 (23.5%) participants reported a clear current implementation status or progress, while 26 (76.5%) reported no clear implementation status. Twenty‐nine (85.3%) participants reported limited or unclear opportunities for strengthening HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination. Nearly all participants, 32 (94.1%), identified challenges affecting policy and strategy implementation, including COVID‐19‐related disruptions and concerns regarding the translation of policies and strategies into practice.ConclusionThe findings indicate a substantial gap between recognition of stakeholder responsibilities and the practical awareness and implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. Strengthening policy dissemination, inclusive stakeholder engagement, implementation monitoring, coordination, and the translation of policy commitments into service‐delivery activities may support progress toward national and global elimination targets. Sustainable financing, strengthened health‐system capacity, stakeholder accountability, and reliable monitoring and evaluation systems are important considerations for improving implementation. 2Methods2.1Study Setting and PeriodThe study was conducted at selected national, regional, and subnational institutions in Ethiopia that are directly involved in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, and delivery of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination services. The study sites included the Ministry of Health (MoH), Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Amhara Public Health Institute (APHI), regional health bureaus, zonal health offices, district health offices, University of Gondar Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, selected health centers, drug stores, and regional blood bank units.These institutions were selected because they represent key stakeholders involved in policy formulation, program coordination, disease surveillance, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, laboratory services, pharmaceutical supply, and implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination interventions. Their inclusion enabled the study to capture perspectives from different levels of the health system and to identify contextual factors influencing the development, implementation, and effectiveness of relevant policies, regulations, and strategies.Data collection was conducted from April 17, 2023, to May 27, 2023. The principal investigator conducted the qualitative data collection using semi‐structured interview and discussion guides developed in accordance with the study objectives. Key informant interviews, in‐depth interviews, and focus group discussions were conducted with relevant stakeholders and participants, while institutional visits and review of relevant policy, strategic, guideline, and regulatory documents were undertaken to complement the interview data.2.2Study DesignA facility‐ and institution‐based qualitative study was conducted to explore the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The study employed an interpretive qualitative approach to obtain in‐depth information from policymakers, program managers, researchers, healthcare professionals, laboratory personnel, pharmacists, and other relevant stakeholders involved in policy development, program implementation, regulation, and service delivery. Data were collected through qualitative interviews and focus group discussions, complemented by a review of relevant policies, strategies, guidelines, and other program documents, as well as observations from selected health‐service and pharmaceutical settings.2.3Study ParticipantThe study participants were purposively selected from key stakeholders involved in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, and delivery of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia. Participants included policymakers and program managers from the Federal Ministry of Health (MoH), regional health bureaus, and zonal and district health offices; researchers and technical experts from the Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Amhara Public Health Institute (APHI), and Ethiopian higher education institutions; healthcare professionals, including physicians, nurses, and other clinical practitioners; laboratory technologists from regional blood bank units and health facilities; pharmacists working in government and private institutions; and other relevant stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and pharmaceutical supply.In addition, individuals receiving HIV, HBV, or HCV‐related healthcare services were included to provide perspectives on service accessibility, utilization, experiences, and challenges encountered at the patient and community levels. Relevant policy, program, and strategic documents were also reviewed to complement the information obtained from participants.Participants were selected based on their knowledge, professional experience, or direct involvement in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development, implementation, regulation, research, or service delivery. Individuals who met the predefined eligibility criteria and voluntarily provided informed consent to participate during the study period were included in the study (Table 1).Table 1Distribution of Sons, Ltd.2.4Sampling and Sampling ProcedureParticipants were selected using purposive sampling, a non‐probability sampling technique appropriate for qualitative research. The selection was based on participants’ knowledge, professional experience, roles, and direct involvement in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, research, or delivery of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia.A total of 34 participants were purposively selected from relevant stakeholder groups, including policymakers and program managers, researchers and technical experts, healthcare professionals, laboratory and blood‐bank personnel, pharmacists, and other stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination. Participant selection was guided by the type of organization, professional role, level of involvement in HIV, HBV, and HCV programs, and relevant experience and expertise.Recruitment continued until data saturation was reached, defined as the point at which additional interviews and discussions no longer generated substantial new information, concepts, or themes relevant to the study objectives. The diversity of participants across national, regional, subnational, research, clinical, laboratory, pharmaceutical, and service‐delivery settings was intended to capture multiple perspectives on the challenges and opportunities affecting the development, implementation, and effectiveness of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia.2.5Data Collection StrategyData were collected in three sequential phases using qualitative methods to explore the challenges and opportunities influencing the development, implementation, and effectiveness of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The qualitative data collection comprised in‐depth interviews (IDIs), key informant interviews (KIIs), and focus group discussions (FGDs), allowing the study to capture individual experiences, stakeholder perspectives, and shared experiences related to HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and elimination. Phase 1: In‐Depth Interviews (IDIs) In‐depth interviews were conducted with individuals living with HIV, including those receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), to explore their experiences and perceptions regarding HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and related health services. The interviews focused on participants’ experiences with healthcare services, access to information and treatment, perceived barriers to service utilization, experiences with healthcare providers, and factors that facilitate or hinder effective implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination interventions.Participants were also encouraged to describe their perceptions of existing HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies and how these policies translate into services at the community and health‐facility levels. Particular attention was given to challenges related to access, affordability, availability of medicines and diagnostic services, stigma and discrimination, continuity of care, and opportunities for improving implementation. Phase 2: Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) Key informant interviews were conducted with policymakers, program managers, health‐system leaders, healthcare professionals, researchers, laboratory professionals, pharmacists, and other stakeholders involved in the planning, coordination, regulation, implementation, and monitoring of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination programs in Ethiopia.The KIIs explored participants’ perspectives on the development and implementation of national HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies; stakeholder roles and responsibilities; coordination mechanisms; availability of financial, human, pharmaceutical, laboratory, and other resources; and the current status of implementation. Participants were also asked to identify major barriers and enabling factors affecting policy implementation at national, regional, and service‐delivery levels.The interviews further explored opportunities for strengthening prevention, case identification, testing and diagnosis, linkage to care, treatment, viral suppression, monitoring, surveillance, and integration of HIV, HBV, and HCV services within the Ethiopian health system. Participants were encouraged to provide recommendations for addressing identified policy, regulatory, organizational, and implementation gaps. Phase 3: Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) Focus group discussions were conducted with healthcare professionals and other relevant stakeholders involved in HIV, HBV, and HCV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, care, and program implementation. The FGDs facilitated discussion of shared experiences, perceptions, and contextual factors influencing the implementation of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies.The discussions explored health‐system challenges, availability of medicines and diagnostic services, human‐resource capacity, provider knowledge and skills, referral and linkage systems, stigma and discrimination, financing, coordination among stakeholders, monitoring and evaluation, and the integration of HIV, HBV, and HCV services. Participants also discussed opportunities to improve implementation and accelerate progress toward national and global control and elimination targets.2.6Trustworthiness of the StudyTo ensure the trustworthiness and methodological rigor of the qualitative study, the principles of credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability were considered throughout the research process.Credibility was enhanced through the use of multiple qualitative data sources, including in‐depth interviews (IDIs), key informant interviews (KIIs), focus group discussions (FGDs), document review, and direct observation of relevant service and pharmacy settings. These complementary sources enabled triangulation of information and provided opportunities to compare perspectives across different participant groups and sources. The semi‐structured interview and discussion guides were developed based on the study objectives, reviewed by subject‐matter experts, and pre‐tested in a non‐study setting to improve their clarity, relevance, and applicability. Experienced qualitative researchers conducted the data collection following standardized procedures, and regular supervision and debriefing were undertaken to enhance consistency and data quality.Transferability was supported by providing detailed descriptions of the study context, participant groups, data‐collection procedures, and the policy and health‐system environment in which HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies were implemented. Such contextual descriptions enable readers and researchers to assess the applicability of the findings to similar settings.Dependability was strengthened through the systematic application of standardized data‐collection procedures, researcher training, close supervision, and documentation of methodological decisions throughout the study. The development, review, and pre‐testing of the interview guides, together with regular debriefing sessions, helped maintain consistency across IDIs, KIIs, and FGDs. The research team also reviewed transcripts and translated materials for completeness and consistency before analysis.Confirmability was enhanced by maintaining a close connection between the findings and the original participant accounts. Audio recordings were transcribed verbatim, and transcripts were translated into English by bilingual professionals familiar with the study subject matter. A back‐translation procedure was performed on a subset of transcripts to verify translation accuracy and preserve the intended meaning of participants’ responses. full_text_sections.results: 3Results and Discussion3.1Participant CharacteristicsA total of 34 participants were included in the qualitative study. The participants represented diverse stakeholder groups involved in the development, implementation, regulation, research, and delivery of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination interventions in Ethiopia. The mean duration of participants’ professional work experience was 16.82 years (SD = 0.79), indicating substantial professional experience among the informants.The majority of participants were male (30, 88%), while 4 (12%) were female. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionThis study explored stakeholder perspectives on the development, implementation, opportunities, and challenges related to HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The findings demonstrate an important discrepancy between recognition of stakeholder responsibilities and the practical visibility and implementation of policies. Although 94.1% of participants demonstrated an understanding of stakeholder roles, only 35.3% clearly identified the existence and key features of relevant policies, 44.1% reported stakeholder involvement in policy and strategy development, and only 23.5% reported a clear current implementation status. Furthermore, 85.3% perceived limited opportunities for strengthening hepatitis elimination activities, while 94.1% identified challenges affecting implementation. Taken together, these findings suggest that the principal issue is not simply the absence of policy documents, but the extent to which policies are communicated, translated into operational activities, monitored, financed, and coordinated across different levels of the health system.4.1Awareness of HIV, HBV, and HCV Policies, Regulations, and StrategiesOnly 35.3% of participants in this study clearly identified or described the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies, whereas 64.7% did not clearly identify or describe them. This finding is consistent with earlier Ethiopian evidence showing that, although Ethiopia had begun developing hepatitis strategic plans and guidelines, the national response was characterized by limited coordination, inadequate dissemination of guidance, weak surveillance, and limited access to hepatitis services. In their qualitative assessment of Ethiopia's hepatitis response, Abera et al. reported that the country was developing strategic plans and guidelines but lacked sufficient partnerships and resource mobilization, while treatment and screening guidelines were not adequately available or implemented [5].The finding is also consistent with more recent evidence showing that knowledge and awareness do not necessarily translate into appropriate hepatitis‐related practices in Ethiopia. For example, a systematic review and meta‐analysis of 26 Ethiopian studies reported that only 47.45% of participants had a good level of knowledge concerning HBV prevention, while good preventive practices were reported in only 36.22% (2026). Although that evidence concerns individual‐level knowledge rather than awareness of national policies, it supports the broader observation that information and communication gaps remain relevant to hepatitis prevention and control in Ethiopia.Evidence from other settings similarly demonstrates that policy formulation does not automatically ensure effective policy awareness or implementation. A global assessment of 55 national viral hepatitis strategic action plans found substantial gaps in alignment with WHO recommendations: 35% of plans did not include HBV and HCV elimination goals, and only 38% included a national budget or financing plan for hepatitis activities [7]. More recent country profiles also show continuing weaknesses in national monitoring and service coverage despite the existence of formal policies. Among 33 countries assessed for HCV elimination, only 55% had systems tracking the number of people tested and treated, while only 30% had achieved the WHO 2025 diagnosis‐coverage target [7, 8].The Ethiopian finding should therefore be interpreted as an implementation‐system issue rather than simply an individual knowledge deficit. The WHO Global Health Sector Strategy 2022–2030 emphasizes that countries need effective strategic information systems capable of generating and analyzing data from service‐delivery and administrative levels to monitor progress toward elimination targets [1]. The low awareness observed in the present study may therefore reflect limited dissemination and operational communication of policy documents between national, regional, and service‐delivery levels.4.2Stakeholder Involvement in Policy and Strategy DevelopmentOnly 44.1% of participants reported involvement of relevant stakeholders in the development of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies, while 55.9% did not report adequate opportunities for participation. This finding is important because WHO's 2022–2030 Global Health Sector Strategies explicitly emphasize leadership, partnerships, multisectoral action, community engagement, and collaboration with stakeholders as central components of the response to HIV and viral hepatitis [1]. The WHO strategy also describes its own development process as broadly consultative, involving Member States, experts, communities, partners, and other stakeholders.The relatively limited stakeholder involvement identified in this study is consistent with the earlier Ethiopian qualitative assessment by Abera et al., which identified inadequate partnerships and limited resource mobilization as important weaknesses in the country's hepatitis response [5]. It also corresponds with evidence from sub‐Saharan Africa showing that operationalizing hepatitis elimination requires coordinated involvement of governments, healthcare providers, technical organizations, professional groups, and development partners. African countries have faced difficulties translating HCV elimination objectives into operational programs because of diagnostic costs, medicine access, logistics, and limited program infrastructure [9].There are also examples demonstrating the potential value of coordinated national and continental approaches. The establishment of the Africa CDC viral hepatitis prevention and control program represents a continental mechanism intended to support countries in developing and strengthening hepatitis elimination program [10]. Similarly, Rwanda and Egypt are among countries that have demonstrated progress in operationalizing hepatitis elimination approaches, although their experiences occur within different health‐system and financing contexts and should not be directly equated with Ethiopia.The finding from this study is therefore relevant to WHO's emphasis on a whole‐of‐government and whole‐of‐society approach. The global strategy recognizes that effective implementation requires political and community leadership and partnerships extending beyond the health sector [1]. Limited participation of stakeholders outside central institutions may reduce opportunities for incorporating service‐delivery experience, research evidence, professional expertise, and community perspectives into policy development.4.3Understanding of Stakeholder RolesA particularly notable finding was that 94.1% of participants demonstrated an understanding of their roles and responsibilities in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy development and implementation. This relatively high recognition contrasts with the lower levels of policy awareness and implementation‐status awareness observed in the same study. Thus, participants appeared to understand what their responsibilities were, even when they had less certainty about which policies were currently being implemented and how much progress had been achieved.This distinction is important in interpreting the findings. The Ethiopian evidence indicates that healthcare professionals can possess substantial hepatitis‐related knowledge while important gaps remain in translating knowledge into practice. For example, a study among healthcare professionals at the University of Gondar Hospital found that 73.1% had good knowledge of HBV transmission, progression, and vaccination, but knowledge varied substantially by professional group [11]. Similarly, the more recent Ethiopian study of healthcare workers found that only 32.5% demonstrated adequate knowledge concerning HBV post‐exposure prophylaxis despite generally positive attitudes.The present finding therefore sug…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6ConclusionMost stakeholders have no information about the availability of hepatitis control and elimination policy, regulations, and strategies, but they effectively understand their role during preparations and implementations of hepatitis control and elimination policy, regulations, and strategies. The policy, regulations, and strategies were not prepared with full involvement of concerned bodies as a result, there is no enough implementations progress reports from the respondents. The existence of hepatitis different guidelines, policies, regulations, strategies, documents, and hepatitis elimination program incorporation to sustainable development goals and vaccine availability for healthcare providers and newborn babies are a good opportunity. Funding problem, lack of training, community culture and belief, COVID‐19, commitments of different stakeholders including government, shortage of medications, lack of awareness and mobilizations, and weak practices of monitoring and evaluations are the most common challenges. Although the COVID‐19 pandemic required immediate public health measures, its effects on hepatitis control initiatives underscore the necessity of comprehensive approaches that tackle both COVID‐19 and persistent viral hepatitis issues. Based on the finding we recommend to revised the existing policy, regulations and strategies with the full invitations of concerned bodies, collaborate with many donor organizations, accessing screening, testing and treatment of the patients, practical performing of monitoring and evaluations, increase the awareness and mobilizations of for patients, health care providers and other concerned bodies are important activities to control and eliminate hepatitis.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remain major public health challenges worldwide and continue to cause substantial morbidity, mortality, and health‐system burden. HBV and HCV can cause acute and chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, while HIV requires lifelong treatment and sustained healthcare services. These infections also share important prevention and health‐system priorities, including safe blood and injection practices, prevention of mother‐to‐child transmission, testing, treatment, monitoring, community engagement, and access to quality health services. Despite major advances in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, gaps remain in translating available interventions into effective population‐level program [1, 2]. In 2022, approximately 254 million people were living with chronic HBV infection and 50 million with HCV infection globally, and viral hepatitis B and C caused approximately 1.3 million deaths, mainly from cirrhosis and liver cancer [2].The burden of viral hepatitis is particularly important in low‐ and middle‐income countries and in the WHO African Region. Although effective prevention, diagnostic, and treatment interventions are available, access remains inadequate in many settings. WHO's Global Health Sector Strategies 2022–2030 established the goal of eliminating viral hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030 and emphasized people‐centered services, health‐system strengthening, strategic information, partnerships, community engagement, and integrated approaches to service delivery [1]. However, recent evidence demonstrates that the global response remains off track. The 2026 WHO Global Hepatitis Report estimated that approximately 1.3 million people died from HBV‐ and HCV‐related cirrhosis and liver cancer in 2024, while treatment coverage for chronic HBV remained below 5% despite the availability of effective antiviral therapy [3]. These findings indicate that the availability of effective interventions alone is insufficient without appropriate policies, financing, governance, stakeholder coordination, monitoring, and implementation systems.Ethiopia has a substantial burden of HBV and HCV and has progressively developed policy and strategic responses to address viral hepatitis. Earlier systematic evidence estimated the pooled prevalence of HBV infection in Ethiopia at 7.4% [3], while an updated systematic review reported a pooled prevalence of approximately 6% [4]. More recent evidence continues to demonstrate a considerable HBV burden, with a systematic review of studies conducted in Ethiopia reporting a pooled prevalence of 6.9%. Previous Ethiopian studies have also identified important gaps in prevention, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance, and health‐system capacity.Ethiopia has recognized viral hepatitis as an important public health problem and has developed policies, strategies, and program structures to address it. A landmark qualitative assessment examined the national response to HBV and HCV using interviews with key informants, policy and strategy document review, and observation of pharmaceutical premises [5]. The study found that Ethiopia was developing strategic plans and guidelines but faced limited partnerships and resource mobilization, inadequate community awareness, restricted availability of screening, insufficient treatment guidance, weak surveillance, and limited availability of effective medicines. The authors concluded that the national response was fragmented and recommended strengthening surveillance, screening, vaccination, treatment, policy guidance, partnerships, and access to affordable medicines. Subsequent research has identified additional opportunities for HCV elimination in Ethiopia, including phased micro‐elimination, task shifting, improved access to affordable diagnostics and direct‐acting antivirals, blood‐safety interventions, and multisectoral collaboration [6].Despite these developments, existing HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies are understood and experienced by stakeholders responsible for their development and implementation at different levels of the Ethiopian health system. In particular, limited recent evidence is available regarding stakeholders’ awareness of existing policies and strategies, their participation in policy development, understanding of roles and responsibilities, perceptions of current implementation status, available opportunities, and challenges affecting implementation. The 2016 Ethiopian policy assessment provided important baseline evidence regarding the national hepatitis response, but the policy and program environment has subsequently evolved, including the development of newer strategic frameworks. Therefore, there is a need for updated evidence examining whether policy commitments are visible and understood by stakeholders and how they are translated into implementation across national, regional, district, and service‐delivery levels.There is limited stakeholder‐level evidence linking the formal existence of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies, regulations, and strategies with their practical implementation, coordination, monitoring, and perceived effectiveness in Ethiopia. The existence of policy documents does not necessarily demonstrate that stakeholders are aware of them, participate in their development, understand their responsibilities, or have adequate resources and institutional mechanisms to implement them. This gap is particularly important because WHO identifies strategic information, accountability, partnerships, financing, community engagement, and integrated service delivery as essential components of achieving the 2030 HIV and viral hepatitis targets [1]. The continuing global shortfall in progress toward viral hepatitis elimination further demonstrates the importance of understanding implementation barriers at country level.To address this gap, the present study explored the challenges and opportunities of HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination policies, regulations, and strategies in Ethiopia. The study examined perspectives from stakeholders involved in policy development, program management, research, regulation, laboratory and pharmaceutical services, healthcare delivery, and other relevant activities. Qualitative interviews and focus group discussions were complemented by review of relevant policies, strategies, guidelines, and program documents and observations of selected health‐service and pharmaceutical settings. Specifically, the study assessed stakeholders’ awareness of policy and strategy existence and features, involvement in policy development, understanding of roles and responsibilities, perceptions of current implementation status, available opportunities, and challenges affecting implementation. By addressing these dimensions, the study provides updated evidence to inform policymakers, program managers, health planners, researchers, professional associations, healthcare providers, and development partners in strengthening policy dissemination, stakeholder engagement, coordination, implementation, monitoring, and accountability toward HIV, HBV, and HCV control and elimination in Ethiopia. 2.1Study Setting and PeriodThe study was conducted at selected national, regional, and subnational institutions in Ethiopia that are directly involved in the development, implementation, regulation, monitoring, and delivery of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) control and elimination services. The study sites included the Ministry of Health (MoH), Ethiopian Public Health Institute (EPHI), Amhara Public Health Institute (APHI), regional health bureaus, zonal health offices, district health offices, University of Gondar Comprehensive Specialized Hospital, selected health centers, drug stores, and regional blood bank units.These institutions were selected because th…

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the challenges and opportunities in the control and elimination of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies in Ethiopia, highlighting the gap between policy recognition and practical implementation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted in Ethiopia from April 17 to May 27, 2023, and involved 34 purposively selected participants representing key stakeholders in HIV, HBV, and HCV policy formulation, implementation, and service delivery.
analysis.methods: Data were collected through qualitative interviews, focus group discussions, and a review of policy, strategy, guideline, and program documents, alongside observations from health-service and pharmaceutical settings.
analysis.main_results: Only 35.3% of participants clearly identified the existence and key features of HIV, HBV, and HCV control policies, while 94.1% understood stakeholder roles, but only 23.5% reported clear implementation status.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings indicate a significant gap between policy recognition and practical implementation, with most participants identifying challenges such as COVID-19 disruptions and lack of translation of policies into practice.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the need for improved policy implementation and stakeholder engagement in Ethiopia to effectively control and eliminate HIV, HBV, and HCV.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the challenges and opportunities in the control and elimination of HIV, HBV, and HCV policies in Ethiopia. Conducted from April 17 to May 27, 2023, it involved 34 purposively selected stakeholders from key institutions. Data were gathered through interviews, focus groups, and document reviews. Results showed that only 35.3% of participants recognized the existence of HBV-related policies, while 94.1% understood stakeholder roles. However, only 23.5% reported clear implementation status. The authors interpret these findings as indicating a substantial gap between policy recognition and practical implementation, with challenges such as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and inadequate translation of policies into practice. The study's qualitative design and purposive sampling limit its generalizability, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估埃塞俄比亚控制和消除艾滋病毒、乙型肝炎和丙型肝炎政策的挑战和机遇,强调政策认识与实际执行之间的差距。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究于 2023 年 4 月 17 日至 5 月 27 日在埃塞俄比亚进行,涉及 34 名特意挑选的参与者,他们代表艾滋病毒、乙型肝炎和丙型肝炎政策制定、实施和服务提供的主要利益相关者。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过定性访谈、焦点小组讨论、政策、战略、指南和项目文件审查以及卫生服务和制药机构的观察来收集数据。
analysis_zh.main_results: 只有 35.3% 的参与者清楚地认识到 HIV、HBV 和 HCV 控制政策的存在及其主要特征,而 94.1% 的参与者了解利益相关者的角色,但只有 23.5% 的参与者报告了明确的实施情况。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 调查结果表明,政策认知与实际实施之间存在巨大差距,大多数参与者都指出了诸如 COVID-19 干扰和缺乏将政策转化为实践等挑战。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果强调,埃塞俄比亚需要改进政策实施和利益相关者参与,以有效控制和消除艾滋病毒、乙肝病毒和丙肝病毒。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其定性性质和有目的的抽样而受到限制,这可能会影响普遍性。由于关注的是利益相关者的观点而不是定量结果,证据是温和的。
