full_text: AbstractBackgroundThe combined effects of donor hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) status and recipient pre-transplant hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) levels on post-transplant HBV events remain unclear in pediatric living donor liver transplantation (LDLT).MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed pediatric LDLT recipients transplanted between May 2018 and June 2023. The primary outcome was the first post-transplant hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive result, with death treated as a competing event. Recipients were stratified by donor anti-HBc status and recipient anti-HBs level (≥100 vs <100 mIU/mL). Antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir (0.015 mg/kg once daily) was given only to recipients of anti-HBc-positive grafts, and hepatitis B immune globulin was not used. Cumulative incidence was compared using Gray’s test, and associated factors were evaluated using Fine–Gray regression.ResultsAmong 229 recipients, 14 (6.1%) developed HBV events. Events occurred in 0 of 97 recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL (G1), 3 of 67 with an anti-HBc-negative donor and anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL (G2), 2 of 29 with an anti-HBc-positive donor and anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL (G3), and 9 of 36 with an anti-HBc-positive donor and anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL (G4); the corresponding 5-year cumulative incidences were 0%, 4.5%, 6.9% and 25.0% (global Gray’s test, P<0.001). Donor anti-HBc positivity (sHR, 8.28; 95% CI, 2.27–30.28; P = 0.001) and recipient anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL (sHR, 6.02; 95% CI, 1.32–27.55; P = 0.021) were independently associated with HBV events, although the wide confidence intervals reflect the small number of events (n = 14) and the magnitude of these estimates should be interpreted with caution.ConclusionsDonor anti-HBc positivity and low recipient pre-transplant anti-HBs were independently associated with post-transplant HBV events after pediatric LDLT. Combined donor–recipient serological stratification identified a clear risk gradient and may support risk-adapted HBV surveillance and prevention.Keywords: anti-HBc, anti-HBs, competing risks, Fine–Gray regression, hepatitis B virus, living donor liver transplantation, pediatric liver transplantation MethodsStudy design and participantsWe conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of pediatric recipients who underwent LDLT between May 2018 and June 2023 at the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China. All consecutive pediatric LDLT recipients during the study period were screened for eligibility.All consecutive pediatric recipients (aged <18 years) who underwent living-donor liver transplantation at our center between May 2018 and June 2023 were screened for eligibility. Recipients who were lost to follow-up and for whom post-transplant HBV outcome status could not be adequately ascertained were excluded. All donors and all recipients were documented as HBsAg-negative before transplantation. Of 237 recipients initially identified, eight were excluded because of loss to follow-up, leaving 229 recipients in the final analytical cohort (Figure 1).Figure 1Study flow diagram. Among 237 pediatric recipients who underwent LDLT between May 2018 and June 2023, eight were excluded because of loss to follow-up. The final analytical cohort comprised 229 recipients, of whom 14 developed a post-transplant HBV event and 215 did not. LDLT, living donor liver transplantation; HBV, hepatitis B virus.Flowchart showing study enrollment: pediatric LDLT recipients cohort from May 2018 to June 2023 with 237 participants. Eight excluded due to lost follow-up, resulting in a final study cohort of 229. Of these, 215 had no HBV event and 14 had an HBV event, with etiological category considered for the HBV event group.Clinical, demographic, transplantation, and laboratory data were retrospectively obtained from electronic medical records.The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University [Approval No. (2026) Lun Shen (Lin Yan) No. (268)]. The requirement for individual patient informed consent was waived because of the retrospective observational design and use of anonymized clinical data. All living-donor organs were obtained through voluntary donation with written informed consent in accordance with applicable national regulations and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.HBV prophylaxis and post-transplant surveillancePerioperative and post-transplant HBV prevention followed the institutional protocol in use at our center during the study period. Consistent with Chinese national immunization requirements, all recipients were scheduled to receive the standard hepatitis B vaccination series (three doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, with the first dose administered within 24 h of birth) before transplantation (14). However, because the majority of recipients were young infants who underwent urgent living-donor liver transplantation, most had received only the first dose, and the extent to which the full series had been completed before transplantation could not be retrospectively verified (15, 16).Hepatitis B immune globulin was not administered in this cohort (17). Post-transplant antiviral prophylaxis was restricted to recipients of anti-HBc-positive grafts (G3 and G4; n = 65), who received entecavir 0.015 mg/kg once daily throughout the perioperative period, on the basis that anti-HBc-positive grafts carry a recognized risk of de novo HBV infection (18). Recipients of anti-HBc-negative grafts (G1 and G2; n = 164) did not receive antiviral prophylaxis. Recipients who developed an HBV event began entecavir at 0.015 mg/kg once daily from the date of the first documented HBsAg-positive result. Antiviral prophylaxis was therefore determined by donor anti-HBc status, but was not modified according to recipient pre-transplant anti-HBs level.HBV serological variables and risk-group definitionsSerum HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc were measured on an Abbott ARCHITECT i2000SR automated immunoassay analyzer and on a Johnson & Johnson Vitros line using chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA). HBsAg is reported in IU/mL and anti-HBs in mIU/mL; anti-HBs values recorded in IU/L were converted according to the international standard. HBeAg, anti-HBe and anti-HBc were determined qualitatively and are expressed as signal-to-cutoff (s/co) ratios. HBV DNA was quantified by real-time fluorescence-based polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using a SLAN-96S automated medical PCR analysis system (Shanghai Hongshi Medical Technology Co., Ltd.) and is reported in IU/mL, with a lower limit of detection of 400 IU/mL.Donor anti-HBc status was classified as positive or negative according to pre-transplant serological testing. Recipient pre-transplant anti-HBs concentration was analyzed as both a continuous variable and a dichotomous variable using a prespecified cutoff of 100 mIU/mL. Anti-HBs concentrations ≥100 mIU/mL were classified as high and concentrations <100 mIU/mL as low (8, 9).Recipients were assigned to four donor–recipient serological groups:G1 comprised recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and recipient anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL.G2 comprised recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and recipient anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL.G3 comprised recipients with an anti-HBc-positive donor and recipient anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL.G4 comprised recipients with an anti-HBc-positive donor and recipient anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL.Recipient pre-transplant anti-HBc status was additionally recorded as a baseline serological characteristic. Because maternal IgG crosses the placenta and may persist through infancy, both a positive anti-HBc result and, to a lesser degree, a detectable anti-HBs concentration in an infant recipient may reflect passively acquired maternal antibody rather than the child’s own infection or immune status. This is of particular relevance when the mother was also the living donor, in which case the maternal and donor serological profiles are inherently linked. Recipient anti-HBc status was therefore not included in the primary multivariable model, and the same consideration was applied when the joint donor–recipient serological patterns were interpreted.Outcome definition and follow-upThe primary outcome was a post-transplant HBV event, defined as the first documented HBsAg-positive result after LDLT. Because HBsAg positivity triggered confirmatory testing in this cohort, HBV DNA and liver biochemistry were measured at the time of the first HBsAg-positive result where available and were used to support, but not to define, the outcome. Events were further characterized according to the duration of HBsAg positivity, the HBV DNA result and the pre-transplant serological profile, so as to distinguish transient antigenemia from sustained infection.Follow-up began on the date of transplantation and continued until the first HBV event, death, the last documented clinical assessment, or the administrative end of follow-up, as applicable. Death occurring before an HBV event was treated as a competing event. Recipients who remained alive without an HBV event were censored at their last observed follow-up.When an HBV event and death occurred on the same recorded date, the recipient was classified as having experienced an HBV event if HBsAg positivity had been documented before or at the assessment preceding death.Among recipients who developed an HBV event, subsequent HBsAg results were reviewed. Documented HBsAg clearance was defined as the first subsequent negative HBsAg result after the initial positive result. Recipients without a documented negative HBsAg result by their final available assessment were classified as having persistent HBsAg positivity.Nested case-series assessmentRecipients who developed a post-transplant HBV event constituted a nested descriptive case series. Individual trajectories from transplantation to the final assessment were reviewed together with recipient age, donor–recipient relationship, donor and recipient pre-transplant HBV serology, and available maternal HBV serology. On the basis of these profiles, cases were categorized into five prespecified exploratory attribution patterns: A, a graft-associated pattern (donor anti-HBc-positive with recipient pre-transplant anti-HBc-negative); B, a graft-associated pattern with possible passive maternal anti-HBc confounding (an anti-HBc-positive mother serving as the donor, with an anti-HBc-positive infant recipient); C, a recipient-side or maternal signal in the presence of an anti-HBc-negative donor; D, indeterminate dual-source attribution; and E, a pattern unexplained by donor or recipient serology (both anti-HBc-negative). Because donor–recipient viral sequence analysis was unavailable, these categories were descriptive and hypothesis-generating and were not used as predictors or outcomes in the primary statistical analyses.Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized as medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), and categorical variables as counts and percentages. Baseline characteristics were compared between recipients with and without post-transplant HBV events. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test and categorical variables using Fisher’s exact test. Because only 14 HBV events occurred, baseline P values were considered descriptive.The cumulative incidence function of post-transplant HBV events was estimated using the Aalen–Johansen estimator, with death before an HBV event treated as a competing event. Cumulative incidence functions were evaluated according to donor anti-HBc status, recipient anti-HBs status dichotomized at 100 mIU/mL, and the four joint donor–recipient serological groups.Equality of cumulative incidence functions was assessed using Gray’s test. Cumulative incidence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported at 1, 2, 3, and 5 years after transplantation.Following a significant global Gray’s test across the four donor–recipient serological groups, all six pairwise Gray’s tests were performed. To account for multiple comparisons, P values were adjusted using the Holm procedure. Both unadjusted and Holm-adjusted P values are presented in Supplementary Table S2, with statistical inference based primarily on the adjusted P values.Fine–Gray proportional subdistribution hazards regression was used to evaluate associations between baseline serological factors and the cumulative incidence of HBV events while accounting for death as a competing event (19). Separate univariable models were fitted for donor anti-HBc positivity and recipient anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL. A multivariable model subsequently included both variables simultaneously.Associations were expressed as subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% CIs and two-sided P values. Given the limited number of HBV events, the multivariable model was intentionally restricted to these two prespecified serological predictors to limit model overfitting.Overall survival was estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method, with recipients alive at the last documented assessment censored at that date. Because only 12 deaths occurred, the survival estimates are descriptive and no between-group test was performed. Given the small number of events (n = 14), the point estimates from the Fine–Gray models are imprecise; the results are therefore interpreted in terms of the direction and consistency of the associations rather than the magnitude of the subdistribution hazard ratios. Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.5.1. full_text_sections.methods: MethodsStudy design and participantsWe conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of pediatric recipients who underwent LDLT between May 2018 and June 2023 at the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University, Chongqing, China. All consecutive pediatric LDLT recipients during the study period were screened for eligibility.All consecutive pediatric recipients (aged <18 years) who underwent living-donor liver transplantation at our center between May 2018 and June 2023 were screened for eligibility. Recipients who were lost to follow-up and for whom post-transplant HBV outcome status could not be adequately ascertained were excluded. All donors and all recipients were documented as HBsAg-negative before transplantation. Of 237 recipients initially identified, eight were excluded because of loss to follow-up, leaving 229 recipients in the final analytical cohort (Figure 1).Figure 1Study flow diagram. Among 237 pediatric recipients who underwent LDLT between May 2018 and June 2023, eight were excluded because of loss to follow-up. The final analytical cohort comprised 229 recipients, of whom 14 developed a post-transplant HBV event and 215 did not. LDLT, living donor liver transplantation; HBV, hepatitis B virus.Flowchart showing study enrollment: pediatric LDLT recipients cohort from May 2018 to June 2023 with 237 participants. Eight excluded due to lost follow-up, resulting in a final study cohort of 229. Of these, 215 had no HBV event and 14 had an HBV event, with etiological category considered for the HBV event group.Clinical, demographic, transplantation, and laboratory data were retrospectively obtained from electronic medical records.The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Children’s Hospital of Chongqing Medical University [Approval No. (2026) Lun Shen (Lin Yan) No. (268)]. The requirement for individual patient informed consent was waived because of the retrospective observational design and use of anonymized clinical data. All living-donor organs were obtained through voluntary donation with written informed consent in accordance with applicable national regulations and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.HBV prophylaxis and post-transplant surveillancePerioperative and post-transplant HBV prevention followed the institutional protocol in use at our center during the study period. Consistent with Chinese national immunization requirements, all recipients were scheduled to receive the standard hepatitis B vaccination series (three doses at 0, 1 and 6 months, with the first dose administered within 24 h of birth) before transplantation (14). full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this single-center cohort of 229 pediatric LDLT recipients, post-transplant HBV events occurred in 14 recipients. Three principal findings emerged. First, donor anti-HBc positivity was strongly associated with subsequent HBV events. Second, recipient pre-transplant anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL was independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of HBV events. Third, joint consideration of these two serological characteristics identified a marked risk gradient: no events occurred among recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL, whereas one-quarter of recipients with both donor anti-HBc positivity and anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL developed an HBV event.The association between donor anti-HBc positivity and post-transplant HBsAg positivity is biologically plausible. Anti-HBc positivity reflects previous HBV exposure, and HBV covalently closed circular DNA may persist within hepatocytes despite the absence of detectable circulating HBsAg (4, 20, 21). The immunosuppressive environment after liver transplantation may permit renewed viral replication from such intrahepatic reservoirs (22). Our findings extend this concern to pediatric LDLT, in which parental living donors constitute the majority of available donors and exclusion of otherwise suitable anti-HBc-positive donors may substantially restrict donor availability.Recipient humoral immunity appeared to modify the observed risk profile. Recipients with pre-transplant anti-HBs <100 mIU/mL had a substantially higher subdistribution hazard of HBV events than those with higher antibody concentrations (23). Nevertheless, anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL did not provide absolute protection: two events occurred among recipients of anti-HBc-positive grafts despite anti-HBs concentrations above this threshold (8, 9). Thus, anti-HBs should probably be viewed as one component of risk stratification rather than as a binary marker of complete protection.Joint stratification provided additional clinically interpretable information. The lowest-risk pattern was observed in G1, in which no HBV events occurred, whereas G4 had a 5-year cumulative incidence of 25.0%. G2 and G3 demonstrated intermediate cumulative incidences, consistent with prior reports in pediatric and adult LDLT cohorts (24–26). This graded distribution suggests that both graft-related HBV exposure and recipient antibody status contribute to the observed post-transplant risk. However, because a formal statistical interaction between donor anti-HBc and recipient anti-HBs was not tested, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating biological or statistical interaction.Our findings are consistent with previous pediatric and adult LDLT series of anti-HBc-positive grafts, which have reported that donor anti-HBc positivity confers a substantial risk of de novo HBV infection while recipient anti-HBs appears partially protective (7, 23–26). Unlike most earlier reports, in which recipients were predominantly adults receiving deceased-donor grafts, the present cohort consisted almost entirely of infants receiving parental living-donor grafts, a setting in which the exclusion of anti-HBc-positive donors would substantially reduce donor availability. The absence of any event among recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL is likewise in keeping with the low risk reported for this combination.Recipient pre-transplant anti-HBc positivity was substantially more common among recipients who subsequently developed HBV events. Interpretation of this association is particularly challenging in the present pediatric cohort because almost 90% of recipients were ≤12 months old. Maternal IgG anti-HBc can cross the placenta and persist during infancy; consequently, a positive pre-transplant anti-HBc result in a young child does not necessarily demonstrate previous HBV infection. This was the principal reason that recipient anti-HBc status was not incorporated into the primary multivariable model.The nested case series further illustrates this interpretive complexity. Seven of 14 event cases displayed a relatively straightforward donor-positive/recipient-negative anti-HBc pattern compatible with a graft-associated source. Other cases, however, demonstrated overlapping donor, recipient, and maternal serological findings. In infants receiving maternal grafts, recipient anti-HBc positivity may reflect passive maternal antibody, whereas in recipients of paternal grafts, independent maternal HBV exposure may provide an alternative explanation. One case occurred despite both donor and recipient being anti-HBc negative. Because donor–recipient viral sequence analysis was unavailable, these classifications were descriptive and hypothesis-generating and were not used as predictors or outcomes in the primary statistical analyses. Serology alone cannot establish the source of individual post-transplant HBV events (27). Viral sequencing or other molecular linkage approaches would be required for definitive source attribution (4, 20).HBsAg clearance was documented in 7 of the 14 recipients (50.0%), with a median time to clearance of 310 days (range 39–819 days). Several factors may account for this heterogeneity. All recipients who developed an event began entecavir at the time of detection, and in at least one instance antigen clearance was accompanied by HBeAg loss and a rise in anti-HBc, consistent with antiviral suppression of a newly established infection. Younger age and a correspondingly greater degree of immunological naivety may favor a tolerant, high-replication state with persistent antigenemia, whereas older children — as illustrated by the three recipients aged 82–132 months in this series — appeared more likely to clear antigen. Age at transplantation did not differ between recipients who did and did not clear HBsAg, and larger cohorts will be required to identify the determinants of outcome.The clinical implications of these findings are primarily risk-stratification oriented. Recipients with both an anti-HBc-positive donor and low pre-transplant anti-HBs constituted the highest-risk subgroup in this cohort and may warrant particularly close HBV surveillance and optimization of preventive strategies (28, 29). The present observational data, however, should not by themselves be used to define a specific antiviral prophylaxis regimen or to exclude anti-HBc-positive living donors. Notably, antiviral monotherapy without hepatitis B immune globulin is consistent with recent reports of a low frequency of HBsAg reemergence after withdrawal of hepatitis B immune globulin (30). Evaluation of prophylactic treatment must take into account the institutional vaccination, hepatitis B immune globulin, antiviral, and monitoring protocols applied during the study period (31–35).With an overall event proportion of 6.1%, the present data do not support universal antiviral prophylaxis in pediatric LDLT. They instead support risk-adapted management. Recipients of anti-HBc-positive grafts with low pre-transplant anti-HBs constituted the highest-risk subgroup and may warrant the most intensive surveillance, whereas recipients with an anti-HBc-negative donor and anti-HBs ≥100 mIU/mL had no events during follow-up and may require less frequent monitoring. Because prophylaxis in this cohort was confined to recipients of anti-HBc-positive grafts, and because events still occurred in that group, whether prophylaxis should be intensified — by extending antiviral therapy, by adding hepatitis B immune globulin, or by active immunization — remains an open question that can only be answered prospectively.Several limitations should be considered. First, this was a retrospective single-center study, which limits generalizability. Second, only 14 HBV events occurred, resulting in wide confidence intervals and limiting the number of variables that could be incorporated into multivariable analysis. Conflict of interest: None. 만성 B형간염에서 Bepirovirsen 3상 임상시험: 기간 한정 치료를 통한 기능적 완치의 가능성 이순규1,2 가톨릭대학교 의과대학 인천성모병원 내과학교실 소화기내과1, 가톨릭대학교 의과대학 간연구소2 Phase 3 Trials of Bepirovirsen in Chronic Hepatitis B: Toward Functional Cure with Finite Therapy Soon Kyu Lee1,2 Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Department of Internal Medicine, Incheon St. Mary’s Hospital, College of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea1; The Catholic University Liver Research Center, Collage of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea2, Seoul, Korea Article: Phase 3 results of bepirovirsen treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection. (N Engl J Med 2026;394:2395-2406) 요약: 만성 B형간염(chronic hepatitis B, CHB) 치료의 궁극 적 목표는 HBsAg 소실로 정의되는 기능적 완치(functional cure)이지만, 현재 표준치료인 뉴클레오시(티)드 유사체 (nucleos(t)ide analogue, NA)로는 이를 달성하기 어렵다. Bepirovirsen은 모든 HBV 전사체(transcript)를 표적으로 하는 안티센스 올리고뉴클레오티드(antisense oligonucleotide, ASO)로, HBV DNA와 HBsAg를 직접 감소시킬 뿐 아니라 선천면역 활성화를 통한 면역조절 효과도 가진다. 본 연구는 NA 치료로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자에서 bepirovirsen의 효능과 안전성을 평가한, 동 일한 설계의 두 개의 3상 무작위 위약대조 이중맹검 시험 (B-Well 1, B-Well 2)이다.1 한국을 포함한 29개국에서 총 1,838명이 등록되었다. 대상은 6개월 이상 NA를 안정적으로 복용 중이면서 HBsAg 100 초과 3,000 IU/mL 이하, HBV DNA <90 IU/mL, ALT가 정상상한치(upper limit of nor- mal, ULN)의 2배 이하인 성인이었으며, 간경변증(의심 포함), C형간염·HIV·D형간염 동시감염, 혈관염 또는 자가면역질환 병력, 혈소판 <140,000/mm3인 환자는 제외하였다. 환자는 선별 시 HBsAg 수치(≤1,000 vs. >1,000 IU/mL)로 층화하 여 2:1로 무작위 배정되었고, bepirovirsen 300 mg 또는 위 약을 24주간 매주 피하주사로 투여받았으며 이 기간 동안 NA는 유지되었다. 이후 NA 단독 유지 기간을 거쳐, 24주부 터 46주까지 HBV DNA가 정량하한(lower limit of quantifi- cation, LLOQ; <20 IU/mL) 미만이고 HBsAg가 미검출 (<0.05 IU/mL)로 지속되며 46주째 ALT ≤2×ULN이고 HBeAg 음성인 환자는 48주에 NA를 중단하였다. 일차 결과 변수는 72주째 기능적 완치(HBV DNA <LLOQ, HBsAg 미 검출, 구제치료 없음)였으며, 주요 이차 결과변수는 HBsAg Lee SK. Bepirovirsen for Functional Cure of Chronic Hepatitis B 481 Vol. 86 No. 4, October 2026 ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서의 기능적 완치와 NA 중단 후 72주째 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지였다. 기저 특성은 양 군에서 유사하였다. 평균 연령은 약 49세, 남성이 71%, 아시아인이 67%, HBeAg 음성이 92%였고, 전 체의 63%가 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL이었다. 48주째 NA 중단 기준을 충족한 환자는 bepirovirsen군의 24%였고 위약군에 서는 없었다. 72주째 기능적 완치율은 B-Well 1에서 bepir- ovirsen군 20% (127/650명) vs. 위약군 0% (0/328명), B-Well 2에서 19% (106/570명) vs. 0% (0/286명)로 두 시험 모두에서 유의하게 높았다(common risk difference 각각 17.5% [95% CI 14.6-20.3], 13.3% [95% CI 10.4-16.1]; 모두 p<0.001). 기저 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 기능적 완 치율이 각각 25%, 28%로 더 높았던 반면, >1,000 IU/mL 층 에서는 10%, 5%에 그쳤다. NA 중단 후 72주째 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지는 두 시험 모두 bepirovirsen군의 23%에서 달 성되었고(HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 29%, 33%), NA 를 중단한 295명 중 5명(2%)에서 HBV DNA가 재검출 (<2,000 IU/mL)되었으나 바이러스학적 또는 임상적 재발은 없었다. 기능적 완치를 달성한 환자에서 HBsAg는 대체로 12 주 이내에 미검출에 도달하였고, 완치 환자의 64–67%에서 anti-HBs가 형성되었다. 기저 HBeAg 양성 환자(전체의 8%) 에서는 기능적 완치가 5–11%에서 관찰되었다. 안전성 측면에서 치료기간(1–24주) 중 이상반응은 bepir- ovirsen군 89%, 위약군 65%에서 보고되었고, 3등급 이상 이 상반응은 16% vs. 3%, 중대한 이상반응은 4% vs. 1%였으며, 이상반응으로 인한 영구 중단은 3%였다. 가장 흔한 이상반응 은 대부분 경증인 주사부위반응(53% vs. 14%)이었다. ALT ≥3×ULN 상승은 bepirovirsen군의 24%에서 주로 5–10주에 HBsAg 감소와 동반되어 나타났으며, 약제유발 간손상 기준 을 충족한 예는 없었다. 혈소판 수와 사구체여과율의 일시적 감소, 피부 혈관염 등 면역 관련 이상반응이 관찰되었으나 대 부분 가역적이었고 투여 보류·중단이 필요한 경우는 1% 미만 이었다. 저자들은 NA를 유지하면서 bepirovirsen을 24주간 투여한 후 기준을 충족한 환자에서 NA를 중단하는 전략으로, NA로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자의 일부에 서 기능적 완치를 유도할 수 있으며, NA 지속 치료 대비 부가 적인 이득을 보여준다고 결론지었다. 해설: 2026년 개정된 대한간학회(Korean Association for the Study of the Liver, KASL) 만성 B형간염 진료 가이드라 인은 항바이러스 치료의 현실적인 단기 목표를 혈청 HBV DNA의 지속적 불검출로, 장기 목표를 HBsAg 소실 또는 혈 청전환으로 정의되는 기능적 완치로 제시하고 있다.2 HBsAg 소실은 HBV DNA 억제만으로 얻을 수 있는 이득을 넘어 간 세포암종(hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC) 발생 위험을 추 가로 낮추며,3 NA 치료 중 HBsAg 소실을 달성한 환자에서는 대부분 소실이 지속되고 HCC 발생률도 낮다.4 그러나 현재 권고되는 NA로 기능적 완치를 달성하는 비율은 약 1–5%에 불과하며 연간 HBsAg 소실률은 0.33% 이하이다.2 국내에서 엔테카비어 또는 테노포비어로 치료받은 852명을 평균 6.3년 추적한 저자의 연구에서도 기능적 완치율은 2.28%에 그쳤 다.5 이러한 배경에서 2022년 AASLD-EASL 치료 종말점 회 의는 기간 한정 치료 종료 24주 후의 HBsAg 소실과 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지를 신약 임상시험의 일차 종말점으로 권고 하였고,6 본 연구는 이 정의를 채택하였다. Bepirovirsen은 국내 연구자들이 참여한 2상 시험에서 안 전성과 항바이러스 효과가 확인되었고,7 2b상 B-Clear 연구에 서 300 mg을 24주간 투여하였을 때 치료 종료 24주 후 기능 적 완치율이 9–10%로 보고되었다.8 KASL 2026 가이드라인 도 기능적 완치를 위한 신약 항목에서 RNA 표적 치료제인 ASO와 소간섭 RNA (small interfering RNA, siRNA)를 소 개하면서 bepirovirsen은 최대 10%의 기능적 완치율로 기술 하고 있고, xalnesiran은 peginterferon alfa-2a 병용군에서 치료 종료 24주 후 기능적 완치율을 23%로 기술하고 있다.2,9 본 3상 연구에서는 기능적 완치율이 약 20%로 확인되었을 뿐 아니라, 기저 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL인 환자에서는 25– 28%의 기능적 완치율을 보여주었다. 특히 동일한 설계의 두 시험에서 결과가 재현되었고, 아시아인이 3분의 2를 차지하 는 대규모 다국가 코호트에 한국 기관이 참여하였다는 점에서 유전자형 C가 대부분인 국내 환자에게도 적용 가능한 근거로 평가할 수 있다. 다만 기저 HBsAg >1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 기능적 완치율이 5–10%로 낮았으므로, 치료 대상 선정에서 정량 HBsAg의 역할이 결정적이다. KASL 가이드라인은 치 료 대상이 아닌 환자에서 12개월마다 HBsAg 정량 또는 정성 검사를 권고하고 있으나,2 앞으로는 NA 치료 중인 환자에서 도 정량 HBsAg를 주기적으로 측정하여 기간 한정 치료의 후 보군을 선별하는 전략이 필요할 것으로 사료된다. 본 연구의 또 다른 의의는 NA 중단 전략과의 연관성이다. KASL 2026 가이드라인은 HBsAg 소실이 2회 이상 확인된 경우에만 NA 중단을 권고하며(A1), 유전자형 C가 대부분인 국내에서는 NA 중단 후 바이러스학적 재발과 간염 악화 위험 이 높다는 점을 들어 신중하고 개별화된 접근을 권고하고 있 다.2 실제로 다국가 RETRACT-B 코호트에서는 NA 중단 시 점의 HBsAg ≥100 IU/mL가 간염 악화의 주요 위험인자였 고, 비아시아인에 비해 아시아인에서 중단 후 HBsAg 소실률 이 낮았다.10,11 본 연구는 24주부터 46주까지 약 6개월간 HBsAg 미검출과 HBV DNA <LLOQ가 지속된 경우에만 48 주에 NA를 중단하도록 설계하였는데, 이는 최소 6개월 간격 의 2회 이상 HBsAg 소실 확인 후 중단을 권고하는 KASL 482 이순규. Bepirovirsen을 통한 만성 B형간염의 기능적 완치 The Korean Journal of Gastroenterology 가이드라인의 원칙과 부합한다.2 그 결과 NA를 중단한 환자 의 2%에서만 저농도의 HBV DNA 재검출이 있었고 임상적 재발은 없었다. 즉 bepirovirsen으로 유도된 HBsAg 소실을 확인한 뒤 NA를 중단하는 전략은 국내 가이드라인의 원칙을 유지하면서도 평생 NA 치료에서 벗어날 수 있는 현실적인 경로를 제시한다. 물론 NA 중단 후에는 가이드라인이 권고하 는 대로 첫 6개월간 1–3개월 간격의 간기능 검사와 HBV DNA 모니터링이 뒤따라야 한다.2 안전성 측면에서 몇 가지 주의가 필요하다. 첫째, bepir- ovirsen 투여 초기의 ALT 상승은 HBsAg의 급격한 감소와 동반되어 나타나며 숙주 면역반응에 의한 감염 간세포 제거를 반영하는 치료 반응의 지표로 해석되고 있으나,12 KASL 가이드 라인이 지적하듯 급성 간염과 유사한 ALT 급상승에 대한 면밀 한 감시가 필요하다.2 본 연구가 간경변증(의심 포함)과 혈소판 <140,000/mm3인 환자를 제외하였으므로, 실제 임상에서도 대상은 간경변이 없는 환자로 제한되어야 한다. 둘째, 24주 동안 매주 2개의 피하주사를 맞아야 하는 치료 부담과 향후 국내 도입 시의 비용 및 급여 문제도 고려해야 할 것이다. 본 연구의 제한점으로는 72주 이후 반응의 지속성이 아직 보고되지 않았다는 점(96주까지의 추적과 B-Sure 연구가 진 행 중), 약 80%의 환자는 여전히 기능적 완치에 도달하지 못 하였다는 점, HBeAg 양성 환자가 8%에 불과하고 간경변 환 자가 제외되었다는 점을 들 수 있다. 저자들은 기능적 완치율 을 높이기 위한 전략으로 siRNA와의 순차 치료(B-United)가 진행 중임을 소개하였으며, bepirovirsen 후 페그인터페론을 순차 투여한 2b상 B-Together 연구에서는 치료 후 재발을 줄일 가능성이 보고되었다.13 아울러 KASL 가이드라인이 언 급한 정량 HBsAg, HBcrAg, HBV RNA 등의 바이오마커를 활용하여 반응 예측 인자를 규명하는 연구도 필요할 것이다.2 결론적으로 본 연구는 NA를 유지하면서 bepirovirsen을 24주간 투여한 후 48주째 기준을 충족한 환자에서 NA를 중 단하는 전략으로, NA로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자의 약 20%에서 72주째 기능적 완치를 달성할 수 있음을 처음으로 3상 시험에서 입증하였으며, 평생 NA 치료 라는 기존 패러다임에서 벗어날 수 있는 가능성을 보여주었 다. 국내 임상에서는 NA 치료 중인 간경변이 없는 환자에서 정량 HBsAg를 측정하여 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL의 후보군 을 미리 파악해 두는 것이 향후 이러한 신약 치료를 적용하기 위한 첫걸음이 될 것이다. 아울러 장기 추적을 통한 반응의 지속성 확인과 함께 국내 환자에서의 실제 치료 자료가 축적 된다면, 기능적 완치를 목표로 하는 치료가 국내 진료 현장에 자리 잡는 데 중요한 근거가 될 것이다. Conflict of interest: None. 만성 B형간염에서 Bepirovirsen 3상 임상시험: 기간 한정 치료를 통한 기능적 완치의 가능성 이순규1,2 가톨릭대학교 의과대학 인천성모병원 내과학교실 소화기내과1, 가톨릭대학교 의과대학 간연구소2 Phase 3 Trials of Bepirovirsen in Chronic Hepatitis B: Toward Functional Cure with Finite Therapy Soon Kyu Lee1,2 Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, Department of Internal Medicine, Incheon St. Mary’s Hospital, College of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea1; The Catholic University Liver Research Center, Collage of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea2, Seoul, Korea Article: Phase 3 results of bepirovirsen treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection. (N Engl J Med 2026;394:2395-2406) 요약: 만성 B형간염(chronic hepatitis B, CHB) 치료의 궁극 적 목표는 HBsAg 소실로 정의되는 기능적 완치(functional cure)이지만, 현재 표준치료인 뉴클레오시(티)드 유사체 (nucleos(t)ide analogue, NA)로는 이를 달성하기 어렵다. Bepirovirsen은 모든 HBV 전사체(transcript)를 표적으로 하는 안티센스 올리고뉴클레오티드(antisense oligonucleotide, ASO)로, HBV DNA와 HBsAg를 직접 감소시킬 뿐 아니라 선천면역 활성화를 통한 면역조절 효과도 가진다. 본 연구는 NA 치료로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자에서 bepirovirsen의 효능과 안전성을 평가한, 동 일한 설계의 두 개의 3상 무작위 위약대조 이중맹검 시험 (B-Well 1, B-Well 2)이다.1 한국을 포함한 29개국에서 총 1,838명이 등록되었다. 대상은 6개월 이상 NA를 안정적으로 복용 중이면서 HBsAg 100 초과 3,000 IU/mL 이하, HBV DNA <90 IU/mL, ALT가 정상상한치(upper limit of nor- mal, ULN)의 2배 이하인 성인이었으며, 간경변증(의심 포함), C형간염·HIV·D형간염 동시감염, 혈관염 또는 자가면역질환 병력, 혈소판 <140,000/mm3인 환자는 제외하였다. 환자는 선별 시 HBsAg 수치(≤1,000 vs. >1,000 IU/mL)로 층화하 여 2:1로 무작위 배정되었고, bepirovirsen 300 mg 또는 위 약을 24주간 매주 피하주사로 투여받았으며 이 기간 동안 NA는 유지되었다. 이후 NA 단독 유지 기간을 거쳐, 24주부 터 46주까지 HBV DNA가 정량하한(lower limit of quantifi- cation, LLOQ; <20 IU/mL) 미만이고 HBsAg가 미검출 (<0.05 IU/mL)로 지속되며 46주째 ALT ≤2×ULN이고 HBeAg 음성인 환자는 48주에 NA를 중단하였다. 일차 결과 변수는 72주째 기능적 완치(HBV DNA <LLOQ, HBsAg 미 검출, 구제치료 없음)였으며, 주요 이차 결과변수는 HBsAg Lee SK. Bepirovirsen for Functional Cure of Chronic Hepatitis B 481 Vol. 86 No. 4, October 2026 ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서의 기능적 완치와 NA 중단 후 72주째 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지였다. 기저 특성은 양 군에서 유사하였다. 평균 연령은 약 49세, 남성이 71%, 아시아인이 67%, HBeAg 음성이 92%였고, 전 체의 63%가 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL이었다. 48주째 NA 중단 기준을 충족한 환자는 bepirovirsen군의 24%였고 위약군에 서는 없었다. 72주째 기능적 완치율은 B-Well 1에서 bepir- ovirsen군 20% (127/650명) vs. 위약군 0% (0/328명), B-Well 2에서 19% (106/570명) vs. 0% (0/286명)로 두 시험 모두에서 유의하게 높았다(common risk difference 각각 17.5% [95% CI 14.6-20.3], 13.3% [95% CI 10.4-16.1]; 모두 p<0.001). 기저 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 기능적 완 치율이 각각 25%, 28%로 더 높았던 반면, >1,000 IU/mL 층 에서는 10%, 5%에 그쳤다. NA 중단 후 72주째 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지는 두 시험 모두 bepirovirsen군의 23%에서 달 성되었고(HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 29%, 33%), NA 를 중단한 295명 중 5명(2%)에서 HBV DNA가 재검출 (<2,000 IU/mL)되었으나 바이러스학적 또는 임상적 재발은 없었다. 기능적 완치를 달성한 환자에서 HBsAg는 대체로 12 주 이내에 미검출에 도달하였고, 완치 환자의 64–67%에서 anti-HBs가 형성되었다. 기저 HBeAg 양성 환자(전체의 8%) 에서는 기능적 완치가 5–11%에서 관찰되었다. 안전성 측면에서 치료기간(1–24주) 중 이상반응은 bepir- ovirsen군 89%, 위약군 65%에서 보고되었고, 3등급 이상 이 상반응은 16% vs. 3%, 중대한 이상반응은 4% vs. 1%였으며, 이상반응으로 인한 영구 중단은 3%였다. 가장 흔한 이상반응 은 대부분 경증인 주사부위반응(53% vs. 14%)이었다. ALT ≥3×ULN 상승은 bepirovirsen군의 24%에서 주로 5–10주에 HBsAg 감소와 동반되어 나타났으며, 약제유발 간손상 기준 을 충족한 예는 없었다. 혈소판 수와 사구체여과율의 일시적 감소, 피부 혈관염 등 면역 관련 이상반응이 관찰되었으나 대 부분 가역적이었고 투여 보류·중단이 필요한 경우는 1% 미만 이었다. 저자들은 NA를 유지하면서 bepirovirsen을 24주간 투여한 후 기준을 충족한 환자에서 NA를 중단하는 전략으로, NA로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자의 일부에 서 기능적 완치를 유도할 수 있으며, NA 지속 치료 대비 부가 적인 이득을 보여준다고 결론지었다. 해설: 2026년 개정된 대한간학회(Korean Association for the Study of the Liver, KASL) 만성 B형간염 진료 가이드라 인은 항바이러스 치료의 현실적인 단기 목표를 혈청 HBV DNA의 지속적 불검출로, 장기 목표를 HBsAg 소실 또는 혈 청전환으로 정의되는 기능적 완치로 제시하고 있다.2 HBsAg 소실은 HBV DNA 억제만으로 얻을 수 있는 이득을 넘어 간 세포암종(hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC) 발생 위험을 추 가로 낮추며,3 NA 치료 중 HBsAg 소실을 달성한 환자에서는 대부분 소실이 지속되고 HCC 발생률도 낮다.4 그러나 현재 권고되는 NA로 기능적 완치를 달성하는 비율은 약 1–5%에 불과하며 연간 HBsAg 소실률은 0.33% 이하이다.2 국내에서 엔테카비어 또는 테노포비어로 치료받은 852명을 평균 6.3년 추적한 저자의 연구에서도 기능적 완치율은 2.28%에 그쳤 다.5 이러한 배경에서 2022년 AASLD-EASL 치료 종말점 회 의는 기간 한정 치료 종료 24주 후의 HBsAg 소실과 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지를 신약 임상시험의 일차 종말점으로 권고 하였고,6 본 연구는 이 정의를 채택하였다. Bepirovirsen은 국내 연구자들이 참여한 2상 시험에서 안 전성과 항바이러스 효과가 확인되었고,7 2b상 B-Clear 연구에 서 300 mg을 24주간 투여하였을 때 치료 종료 24주 후 기능 적 완치율이 9–10%로 보고되었다.8 KASL 2026 가이드라인 도 기능적 완치를 위한 신약 항목에서 RNA 표적 치료제인 ASO와 소간섭 RNA (small interfering RNA, siRNA)를 소 개하면서 bepirovirsen은 최대 10%의 기능적 완치율로 기술 하고 있고, xalnesiran은 peginterferon alfa-2a 병용군에서 치료 종료 24주 후 기능적 완치율을 23%로 기술하고 있다.2,9 본 3상 연구에서는 기능적 완치율이 약 20%로 확인되었을 뿐 아니라, 기저 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL인 환자에서는 25– 28%의 기능적 완치율을 보여주었다. 특히 동일한 설계의 두 시험에서 결과가 재현되었고, 아시아인이 3분의 2를 차지하 는 대규모 다국가 코호트에 한국 기관이 참여하였다는 점에서 유전자형 C가 대부분인 국내 환자에게도 적용 가능한 근거로 평가할 수 있다. 다만 기저 HBsAg >1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 기능적 완치율이 5–10%로 낮았으므로, 치료 대상 선정에서 정량 HBsAg의 역할이 결정적이다. KASL 가이드라인은 치 료 대상이 아닌 환자에서 12개월마다 HBsAg 정량 또는 정성 검사를 권고하고 있으나,2 앞으로는 NA 치료 중인 환자에서 도 정량 HBsAg를 주기적으로 측정하여 기간 한정 치료의 후 보군을 선별하는 전략이 필요할 것으로 사료된다. 본 연구의 또 다른 의의는 NA 중단 전략과의 연관성이다. KASL 2026 가이드라인은 HBsAg 소실이 2회 이상 확인된 경우에만 NA 중단을 권고하며(A1), 유전자형 C가 대부분인 국내에서는 NA 중단 후 바이러스학적 재발과 간염 악화 위험 이 높다는 점을 들어 신중하고 개별화된 접근을 권고하고 있 다.2 실제로 다국가 RETRACT-B 코호트에서는 NA 중단 시 점의 HBsAg ≥100 IU/mL가 간염 악화의 주요 위험인자였 고, 비아시아인에 비해 아시아인에서 중단 후 HBsAg 소실률 이 낮았다.10,11 본 연구는 24주부터 46주까지 약 6개월간 HBsAg 미검출과 HBV DNA <LLOQ가 지속된 경우에만 48 주에 NA를 중단하도록 설계하였는데, 이는 최소 6개월 간격 의 2회 이상 HBsAg 소실 확인 후 중단을 권고하는 KASL 482 이순규. Bepirovirsen을 통한 만성 B형간염의 기능적 완치 The Korean Journal of Gastroenterology 가이드라인의 원칙과 부합한다.2 그 결과 NA를 중단한 환자 의 2%에서만 저농도의 HBV DNA 재검출이 있었고 임상적 재발은 없었다. 즉 bepirovirsen으로 유도된 HBsAg 소실을 확인한 뒤 NA를 중단하는 전략은 국내 가이드라인의 원칙을 유지하면서도 평생 NA 치료에서 벗어날 수 있는 현실적인 경로를 제시한다. 물론 NA 중단 후에는 가이드라인이 권고하 는 대로 첫 6개월간 1–3개월 간격의 간기능 검사와 HBV DNA 모니터링이 뒤따라야 한다.2 안전성 측면에서 몇 가지 주의가 필요하다. 첫째, bepir- ovirsen 투여 초기의 ALT 상승은 HBsAg의 급격한 감소와 동반되어 나타나며 숙주 면역반응에 의한 감염 간세포 제거를 반영하는 치료 반응의 지표로 해석되고 있으나,12 KASL 가이드 라인이 지적하듯 급성 간염과 유사한 ALT 급상승에 대한 면밀 한 감시가 필요하다.2 본 연구가 간경변증(의심 포함)과 혈소판 <140,000/mm3인 환자를 제외하였으므로, 실제 임상에서도 대상은 간경변이 없는 환자로 제한되어야 한다. 둘째, 24주 동안 매주 2개의 피하주사를 맞아야 하는 치료 부담과 향후 국내 도입 시의 비용 및 급여 문제도 고려해야 할 것이다. 본 연구의 제한점으로는 72주 이후 반응의 지속성이 아직 보고되지 않았다는 점(96주까지의 추적과 B-Sure 연구가 진 행 중), 약 80%의 환자는 여전히 기능적 완치에 도달하지 못 하였다는 점, HBeAg 양성 환자가 8%에 불과하고 간경변 환 자가 제외되었다는 점을 들 수 있다. 저자들은 기능적 완치율 을 높이기 위한 전략으로 siRNA와의 순차 치료(B-United)가 진행 중임을 소개하였으며, bepirovirsen 후 페그인터페론을 순차 투여한 2b상 B-Together 연구에서는 치료 후 재발을 줄일 가능성이 보고되었다.13 아울러 KASL 가이드라인이 언 급한 정량 HBsAg, HBcrAg, HBV RNA 등의 바이오마커를 활용하여 반응 예측 인자를 규명하는 연구도 필요할 것이다.2 결론적으로 본 연구는 NA를 유지하면서 bepirovirsen을 24주간 투여한 후 48주째 기준을 충족한 환자에서 NA를 중 단하는 전략으로, NA로 바이러스가 억제된 간경변이 없는 CHB 환자의 약 20%에서 72주째 기능적 완치를 달성할 수 있음을 처음으로 3상 시험에서 입증하였으며, 평생 NA 치료 라는 기존 패러다임에서 벗어날 수 있는 가능성을 보여주었 다. 국내 임상에서는 NA 치료 중인 간경변이 없는 환자에서 정량 HBsAg를 측정하여 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL의 후보군 을 미리 파악해 두는 것이 향후 이러한 신약 치료를 적용하기 위한 첫걸음이 될 것이다. 아울러 장기 추적을 통한 반응의 지속성 확인과 함께 국내 환자에서의 실제 치료 자료가 축적 된다면, 기능적 완치를 목표로 하는 치료가 국내 진료 현장에 자리 잡는 데 중요한 근거가 될 것이다…

full_text_excerpt: Mary’s Hospital, College of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea1; The Catholic University Liver Research Center, Collage of Medicine, The Catholic University of Korea2, Seoul, Korea Article: Phase 3 results of bepirovirsen treatment for chronic hepatitis B virus infection. 해설: 2026년 개정된 대한간학회(Korean Association for the Study of the Liver, KASL) 만성 B형간염 진료 가이드라 인은 항바이러스 치료의 현실적인 단기 목표를 혈청 HBV DNA의 지속적 불검출로, 장기 목표를 HBsAg 소실 또는 혈 청전환으로 정의되는 기능적 완치로 제시하고 있다.2 HBsAg 소실은 HBV DNA 억제만으로 얻을 수 있는 이득을 넘어 간 세포암종(hepatocellular carcinoma, HCC) 발생 위험을 추 가로 낮추며,3 NA 치료 중 HBsAg 소실을 달성한 환자에서는 대부분 소실이 지속되고 HCC 발생률도 낮다.4 그러나 현재 권고되는 NA로 기능적 완치를 달성하는 비율은 약 1–5%에 불과하며 연간 HBsAg 소실률은 0.33% 이하이다.2 국내에서 엔테카비어 또는 테노포비어로 치료받은 852명을 평균 6.3년 추적한 저자의 연구에서도 기능적 완치율은 2.28%에 그쳤 다.5 이러한 배경에서 2022년 AASLD-EASL 치료 종말점 회 의는 기간 한정 치료 종료 24주 후의 HBsAg 소실과 HBV DNA <LLOQ 유지를 신약 임상시험의 일차 종말점으로 권고 하였고,6 본 연구는 이 정의를 채택하였다. 평균 연령은 약 49세, 남성이 71%, 아시아인이 67%, HBeAg 음성이 92%였고, 전 체의 63%가 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL이었다. 48주째 NA 중단 기준을 충족한 환자는 bepirovirsen군의 24%였고 위약군에 서는 없었다. 0% (0/286명)로 두 시험 모두에서 유의하게 높았다(common risk difference 각각 17.5% [95% CI 14.6-20.3], 13.3% [95% CI 10.4-16.1]; 모두 p<0.001). 기저 HBsAg ≤1,000 IU/mL 층에서는 기능적 완 치율이 각각 25%, 28%로 더 높았던 반면, >1,000 IU/mL 층 에서는 10%, 5%에 그쳤다. full_text: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, with an estimated 254 million people living with chronic infection worldwide in 2022.1 Chronic HBV infection is a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for more than half of HCC cases globally.2 Despite vaccination and antiviral therapy, HBV-related HCC continues to contribute substantially to cancer-related mortality.3,4 Importantly, HBV infection confers a risk of HCC even in the absence of cirrhosis, suggesting direct virus-associated genomic mechanisms beyond inflammation and fibrosis.5 Although HBV lacks a viral oncogene, it can promote tumor development through genetic damage, chromosomal instability, and the expression of viral regulatory elements.3,6 HBV replicates through reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA, generating relaxed circular DNA, which is converted to covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) by host machinery.4,7 Some viral genomes form double-stranded linear DNA, which cannot produce infectious progeny but can integrate into host chromosomes.5 These linear molecules resemble cellular DNA breaks and enter host repair pathways, generating integration-competent viral DNA early in infection.7 HBV integration has been detected as early as 23–49 days after infection, indicating that integration is not merely a late consequence of chronic infection.6 Integrated HBV DNA can remain transcriptionally active and contribute to circulating hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels, thereby promoting immune exhaustion and viral persistence.4,7 HBV lacks an integrase and relies on host DNA repair. Double-stranded linear DNA molecules resemble cellular double-strand breaks and are incorporated into host chromosomes primarily through nonhomologous end joining and microhomology-mediated end joining. Because both pathways are error prone, HBV integration generates small insertions, deletions, and complex virus-host junctions that contribute to chromosomal instability.7,8 Although the initial sites of integration in the host genome are largely random, viral DNA linearization breakpoints occur at specific hotspots (Fig. 1).3 Hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations may undergo clonal expansion.8 HBV integrations are enriched in regions of high chromatin accessibility, active transcription, early replication, and genomic fragility, and the breakpoint pattern can influence which viral genes remain intact after integration.3 This commentary reviews the mechanisms of HBV integration, common HBV breakpoints, and their implications for HCC risk and clinical management. A well-supported mechanism of HBV-driven oncogenesis is enhancer-mediated cis-activation of adjacent host genes. HBV enhancer I (HBV-Enh I) and the X region are preferentially preserved in integrated viral sequences, suggesting positive clonal selection of hepatocytes harboring these integrations.8,9 HBV-Enh I can act in cis to drive the expression of nearby oncogenes, such as telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the MYC proto-oncogene (MYC) (Fig. 2).10 Ectopic MYC overexpression driven by HBV-Enh I integration has been reported to promote HCC cell migration and invasion.10 A preferential breakpoint at the 3′ end of hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx) results in C-terminally truncated HBx variants with enhanced oncogenic potential.9 These 3′-deleted proteins lack regulatory domains involved in p53-dependent transcription, Sp1 binding, and growth suppression, thereby promoting cellular proliferation, transformation, and invasion.9 C-terminally truncated HBx was detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and was associated with venous invasion, increased c-Jun activity, metalloproteinase expression, mitogen-activated protein kinase activation, and cell-cycle dysregulation—features of metastatic potential.9 The generation of C-terminally truncated HBx proteins is supported by experimental and clinical studies, although its relative contribution to human hepatocarcinogenesis remains under investigation. Nontumor liver tissue contains a greater diversity of unique HBV integration sites, which are generally low frequency and nonclonal. In contrast, tumor tissue contains fewer unique integration sites but shows substantially greater clonality, indicating the selective expansion of hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations.3,10 Although HBV integration occurs in only approximately 0.1% of infected hepatocytes, integrated HBV DNA has been detected in 85%–90% of HBV-related HCCs, indicating strong biological selection.10 Integrations in nontumor liver tissue are largely transcriptionally silent, whereas tumor-associated integrations occur near functionally relevant regions.3,8 HBV integration events can also promote hepatocarcinogenesis by inactivating tumor suppressor pathways. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were identified in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs.10 Homozygous deletions of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A) occurred in 2%–12%, retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) alterations in 3%–8%, and p53 mutations in 41% of HBV-related HCCs.10 HBV integration-associated telomeric deletions increase the risk of biallelic inactivation of flanking tumor suppressor genes.11 Truncated HBx can suppress p53-dependent transcriptional activity. Loss of RB1 promotes uncontrolled S-phase entry and cellular proliferation, whereas CDKN2A loss impairs both RB1 and p53 tumor suppressor activity.9 Integrated HBV DNA frequently exists as concatemers that generate unstable virus-host junctions prone to recombination and breakage.11 These events can cause genomic restructuring, including nonhomologous chromosomal fusions, dicentric chromosomes, and megabase-scale deletions.10,11 In one genomic analysis, HBV-mediated telomeric deletion events were identified in 8% of HCCs; 40 structural rearrangements resulted in the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including tumor protein p53 (TP53) and RB1.11 A 14.9-Mb telomeric deletion encompassing TP53, with mutation of the remaining allele, was reported, exemplifying HBV-driven biallelic inactivation.11 In HBV-associated HCC, p53 dysfunction is consistently associated with more aggressive tumor biology and a poorer prognosis.10,11 Nevertheless, current evidence suggests that direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes is less common than enhancer-mediated oncogene activation and integration-associated structural rearrangements. Genome-wide sequencing studies have identified recurrent integration hotspots in HCC involving TERT in 20%–50% of cases, lysine methyltransferase 2B/mixed-lineage leukemia 4 (KMT2B/MLL4) in 1%–10%, and cyclin E1 (CCNE1) in approximately 5%. These frequencies exceed those expected by chance and are associated with clonal expansion and altered gene expression (Table 1).12 | Host locus | Key effect | Mechanism | Frequency in HBV-related HCC | Cohort details | |---|---|---|---|---| | TERT | Telomerase activation through cis-regulatory enhancer hijacking | Strongest recurrent hotspot; supports early clonal advantage and telomere maintenance | 20%–50% | 18/88 (20.5%); 101/426 (23.7%); 39/153 (25.5%); 48/177 (27.1%) | | KMT2B/MLL4 | Histone methyltransferase activity, chromatin remodeling, and epigenetic dysregulation | Recurrent epigenetic driver; promotes tumorigenesis through enhancer/chromatin dysregulation | 2%–11% in large series; higher in some small cohorts | 9/88 (10.2%); 31/426 (7.3%); 16/153 (10.5%); 3/177 (1.7%); 6/27 (22.2%) | | CCNE1 | G1/S transition and replication stress | Supports unscheduled cell-cycle entry and genomic instability | 1%–5% | 4/88 (4.5%); 7/426 (1.6%); 4/177 (2.3%) | | CCNA2 | Cell-cycle progression | Less frequent but recurrent; suggests broader cell-cycle selection beyond CCNE1 | 2% in one major cohort | 8/426 (1.9%) | | MYC and PVT1 region | Oncogene amplification and cis-activation | Viral enhancer donation and structural amplification can activate MYC programs | Recurrent, but the frequency has not been consistently reported across cohorts | – | | TP53 | Structural disruption or deletion rather than hotspot integration | Tumor suppressor alteration associated with uncontrolled proliferation | Recurrent, but the frequency has not been consistently reported across cohorts | – | TERT is the most frequent HBV integration hotspot, with tumor-level frequencies reported as 35.8% (34/95),13 23.7% (101/426),3 and 29.8% (28/94).14TERT integration has been associated with more aggressive tumor behavior.13TERT promoter integrations were rare (3%) in nontumor liver tissue, indicating strong positive selection.13 Insertion of HBV-Enh I into the TERT promoter region increases TERT transcription through cis-activation by recruiting host transcription factors to the chimeric TERT promoter, thereby activating telomerase.13 HBV integration at TERT and TERT promoter mutations or other alterations are generally mutually exclusive, suggesting distinct but functionally redundant mechanisms of telomerase reactivation.15 KMT2B/MLL4 is the second most consistently reported recurrent hotspot. KMT2B and KMT2C encode histone H3 lysine 4 (H3K4) methyltransferases involved in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation.12 Disruption of these genes through HBV integration can lead to dysregulated transcription and aberrant chromatin states. Reported frequencies include 10.5% in a 153-case capture-sequencing series, 7.3% in a 426-case cohort, 10.2% in an 88-case dataset, and 1.7% in a 177-case cohort.12 CCNE1 regulates the G1/S cell-cycle transition, and its overexpression can drive uncontrolled cellular proliferation and genomic instability.12,15 Recurrent CCNE1 integrations were identified in 4 of 88 (4.5%), 7 of 426 (1.6%), and 4 of 177 (2.3%) HBV-related HCCs.12 Integration at CCNE1 can upregulate the gene through the insertion of viral enhancer elements or structural rearrangements; these events were tumor-specific and positively selected.12,14 MYC and plasmacytoma variant translocation 1 (PVT1) are less frequently recognized HBV integration targets.12,15 HBV integration can induce focal MYC amplification through structural rearrangements or enhancer-mediated activation, thereby promoting proliferation, clonal expansion, and chromosomal instability.10,15 Reported frequencies of HBV integration patterns vary substantially among cohorts because of differences in geographic region, HBV genotype, disease stage, viral replication level, and sequencing methodology. Genotype C has been associated with more HBV integration events, greater clonal expansion, and more frequent integration into cancer-associated genes.12,15 A meta-analysis of more than 10,000 patients found that HCC developed in 25% of patients with genotype C versus 13% of those with genotype B.16 Passenger HBV integrations, typically found in nontumor liver tissue, occur randomly at low clonal frequencies, whereas driver integrations can contribute to oncogenesis by activating proto-oncogenes, inactivating tumor suppressors, or inducing genomic instability, thereby conferring a proliferative advantage and promoting clonal expansion.3,8,12,17 Only 3%–5% of HBV integration sites overlap between tumor and adjacent nontumor tissue within the same patient, indicating clonal selection.3,17 Oncogenic integration events may arise early, including in preneoplastic dysplastic nodules, and expand during tumor progression.6,8 HBV acts primarily as a regulatory mutagen by donating enhancer activity that activates adjacent oncogenes and as a structural mutagen by inducing chromosomal instability, telomeric deletions, and copy-number alterations.10,11 Truncated HBx further amplifies oncogenic signaling by suppressing p53-dependent transcription, activating mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and dysregulating the cell cycle.9 Together, these mechanisms may help explain the persistent risk of HCC despite viral suppression and in the absence of cirrhosis. HBV integration occurs early in infection, including in patients with minimal liver injury, particularly during high-level viral replication.6,7 The 2025 American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases/Infectious Diseases Society of America guideline suggests antiviral therapy for patients in the immune-tolerant phase who are older than 40 years or have significant hepatic inflammation or fibrosis; for younger patients interested in earlier treatment, it recommends shared decision-making.18 Because evidence that treatment of otherwise low-risk patients in the immune-tolerant phase reduces HCC risk remains uncertain, the possibility that suppression of high-level HBV replication could reduce insertional mutagenesis and HCC risk warrants prospective evaluation. Another emerging area of investigation is the interaction between HBV integration and the tumor immune microenvironment. Integrated HBV DNA can remain transcriptionally active and produce viral transcripts and proteins, particularly HBsAg and HBx, even when viral replication is suppressed.5,17 These persistently expressed viral antigens may influence local hepatic immune responses, with potential downstream effects on antitumor immunity and responses to immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy.17 This hypothesis warrants evaluation in controlled studies. Although early studies suggested that circulating chimeric HBV-host DNA might enable earlier detection of residual or recurrent disease, clinical implementation remains limited by the need for highly specialized detection methods, methodological heterogeneity, and the lack of standardized assays.17,19 Commercial clinical laboratories currently offer serum HBV DNA quantification and related viral biomarkers but do not offer validated integration-site mapping as a standard-of-care assay.17,19 Detection of recurrent driver integrations involving TERT, KMT2B, or CCNE1 may help distinguish random background integrations from tumor-specific events and clarify whether a lesion is linked to an HBV-driven oncogenic pathway.12,17 Patient-specific HBV-host junction sequences may serve as molecular fingerprints for monitoring recurrence.12,19 However, integration profiling has not been validated for routine prognostic decision-making or for guiding surveillance, resectability, or systemic therapy. HBV integration is an early and intrinsic mechanism of hepatocarcinogenesis that can operate independently of cirrhosis. Although most integrations remain silent, a subset may undergo clonal selection through enhancer-mediated oncogene activation, tumor suppressor disruption, chromosomal instability, and the production of truncated HBx proteins. Thus, integrated HBV DNA can act as both a regulatory and a structural mutagen, potentially helping to explain the persistent risk of HCC in HBV infection despite viral suppression. The mechanisms of HBV integration provide an additional rationale for early and sustained suppression of viral replication. Although currently available nucleos(t)ide analogues do not eliminate preexisting integrations or cccDNA, antiviral therapy may reduce the formation of new integration events by suppressing viral replication and decreasing the generation of integration-competent double-stranded linear DNA intermediates. Observational data show that antiviral therapy is associated with a lower HCC incidence in broader populations with chronic hepatitis B, but whether treatment during the immune-tolerant phase reduces HCC risk remains uncertain.18,20 Large, multicenter, long-term controlled studies are needed to test this hypothesis. Prospective multicenter cohorts are needed to validate associations of specific integration sites—such as TERT, KMT2B, CCNE1, and MYC/PVT1—and tumor suppressor-disrupting structural events with prognosis, recurrence risk, and vascular invasion. Standardized integration assays are also needed to determine whether serial monitoring of circulating HBV-host junction DNA can reliably identify minimal residual disease or early recurrence and whether integration-site analysis improves risk stratification. full_text_sections.full_text: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, with an estimated 254 million people living with chronic infection worldwide in 2022.1 Chronic HBV infection is a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for more than half of HCC cases globally.2 Despite vaccination and antiviral therapy, HBV-related HCC continues to contribute substantially to cancer-related mortality.3,4 Importantly, HBV infection confers a risk of HCC even in the absence of cirrhosis, suggesting direct virus-associated genomic mechanisms beyond inflammation and fibrosis.5 Although HBV lacks a viral oncogene, it can promote tumor development through genetic damage, chromosomal instability, and the expression of viral regulatory elements.3,6 HBV replicates through reverse transcription of pregenomic RNA, generating relaxed circular DNA, which is converted to covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) by host machinery.4,7 Some viral genomes form double-stranded linear DNA, which cannot produce infectious progeny but can integrate into host chromosomes.5 These linear molecules resemble cellular DNA breaks and enter host repair pathways, generating integration-competent viral DNA early in infection.7 HBV integration has been detected as early as 23–49 days after infection, indicating that integration is not merely a late consequence of chronic infection.6 Integrated HBV DNA can remain transcriptionally active and contribute to circulating hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels, thereby promoting immune exhaustion and viral persistence.4,7 HBV lacks an integrase and relies on host DNA repair. Double-stranded linear DNA molecules resemble cellular double-strand breaks and are incorporated into host chromosomes primarily through nonhomologous end joining and microhomology-mediated end joining. Because both pathways are error prone, HBV integration generates small insertions, deletions, and complex virus-host junctions that contribute to chromosomal instability.7,8 Although the initial sites of integration in the host genome are largely random, viral DNA linearization breakpoints occur at specific hotspots (Fig. 1).3 Hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations may undergo clonal expansion.8 HBV integrations are enriched in regions of high chromatin accessibility, active transcription, early replication, and genomic fragility, and the breakpoint pattern can influence which viral genes remain intact after integration.3 This commentary reviews the mechanisms of HBV integration, common HBV breakpoints, and their implications for HCC risk and clinical management. A well-supported mechanism of HBV-driven oncogenesis is enhancer-mediated cis-activation of adjacent host genes. HBV enhancer I (HBV-Enh I) and the X region are preferentially preserved in integrated viral sequences, suggesting positive clonal selection of hepatocytes harboring these integrations.8,9 HBV-Enh I can act in cis to drive the expression of nearby oncogenes, such as telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) and the MYC proto-oncogene (MYC) (Fig. 2).10 Ectopic MYC overexpression driven by HBV-Enh I integration has been reported to promote HCC cell migration and invasion.10 A preferential breakpoint at the 3′ end of hepatitis B virus X protein (HBx) results in C-terminally truncated HBx variants with enhanced oncogenic potential.9 These 3′-deleted proteins lack regulatory domains involved in p53-dependent transcription, Sp1 binding, and growth suppression, thereby promoting cellular proliferation, transformation, and invasion.9 C-terminally truncated HBx was detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and was associated with venous invasion, increased c-Jun activity, metalloproteinase expression, mitogen-activated protein kinase activation, and cell-cycle dysregulation—features of metastatic potential.9 The generation of C-terminally truncated HBx proteins is supported by experimental and clinical studies, although its relative contribution to human hepatocarcinogenesis remains under investigation. Nontumor liver tissue contains a greater diversity of unique HBV integration sites, which are generally low frequency and nonclonal. In contrast, tumor tissue contains fewer unique integration sites but shows substantially greater clonality, indicating the selective expansion of hepatocytes harboring oncogenic integrations.3,10 Although HBV integration occurs in only approximately 0.1% of infected hepatocytes, integrated HBV DNA has been detected in 85%–90% of HBV-related HCCs, indicating strong biological selection.10 Integrations in nontumor liver tissue are largely transcriptionally silent, whereas tumor-associated integrations occur near functionally relevant regions.3,8 HBV integration events can also promote hepatocarcinogenesis by inactivating tumor suppressor pathways. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were identified in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs.10 Homozygous deletions of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A) occurred in 2%–12%, retinoblastoma 1 (RB1) alterations in 3%–8%, and p53 mutations in 41% of HBV-related HCCs.10 HBV integration-associated telomeric deletions increase the risk of biallelic inactivation of flanking tumor suppressor genes.11 Truncated HBx can suppress p53-dependent transcriptional activity. Loss of RB1 promotes uncontrolled S-phase entry and cellular proliferation, whereas CDKN2A loss impairs both RB1 and p53 tumor suppressor activity.9 Integrated HBV DNA frequently exists as concatemers that generate unstable virus-host junctions prone to recombination and breakage.11 These events can cause genomic restructuring, including nonhomologous chromosomal fusions, dicentric chromosomes, and megabase-scale deletions.10,11 In one genomic analysis, HBV-mediated telomeric deletion events were identified in 8% of HCCs; 40 structural rearrangements resulted in the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including tumor protein p53 (TP53) and RB1.11 A 14.9-Mb telomeric deletion encompassing TP53, with mutation of the remaining allele, was reported, exemplifying HBV-driven biallelic inactivation.11 In HBV-associated HCC, p53 dysfunction is consistently associated with more aggressive tumor biology and a poorer prognosis.10,11 Nevertheless, current evidence suggests that direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes is less common than enhancer-mediated oncogene activation and integration-associated structural rearrangements. title_original: Hepatitis B Virus Insertional Mutagenesis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Mechanisms and Clinical Significance

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the mechanisms by which hepatitis B virus (HBV) insertional mutagenesis contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and its clinical significance. The background highlights the role of HBV integration in oncogenesis and the need to understand its impact on tumor biology.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study analyzed HBV integration patterns in both nontumor and tumor liver tissues, focusing on the clonality and diversity of integration sites. It examined patients with HBV-related HCC and compared them with non-HBV-related HCC cases to assess the association between integration events and tumor suppressor gene alterations.
analysis.methods: Genome-wide sequencing was used to identify recurrent integration hotspots in HCC, including TERT, KMT2B/MLL4, and CCNE1. The study also evaluated the frequency and impact of HBV integration on tumor suppressor pathways through analysis of breakpoints and truncation of HBx proteins.
analysis.main_results: C-terminally truncated HBx proteins were detected in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases and were linked to features of metastatic potential. Tumor suppressor alterations, including mutations and deletions, were found in up to 48% of HBV-related tumors, compared with 16% of non-HBV-related HCCs. HBV integration events were associated with the deletion or inactivation of 244 tumor suppressor genes, including TP53 and RB1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that HBV integration contributes to hepatocarcinogenesis through both direct disruption of tumor suppressor genes and enhancer-mediated oncogene activation. The study highlights the importance of integration-associated structural rearrangements in promoting aggressive tumor biology.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results have implications for improving the detection and monitoring of HBV-driven oncogenic pathways in HCC. They also emphasize the need for integration-site analysis to better understand the mechanisms of HBV-related hepatocarcinogenesis and guide clinical decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on observational data and does not establish causality. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on genomic analysis and clinical observations without experimental validation of the causal relationship between HBV integration and HCC progression.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the mechanisms of hepatitis B virus (HBV) insertional mutagenesis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), emphasizing its role in oncogenesis. It identifies C-terminally truncated HBx proteins in up to 79.3% of HBV-associated HCC cases, linked to metastatic features. The research also highlights the impact of HBV integration on tumor suppressor genes, such as TP53 and RB1, through structural rearrangements. These findings suggest that integration events are critical in HBV-related HCC progression, though the evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and lack of experimental validation. The study underscores the need for standardized integration assays to improve risk stratification and monitoring of HBV-driven oncogenic pathways in HCC.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨乙型肝炎病毒(HBV)插入突变导致肝细胞癌(HCC)的机制及其临床意义。这一背景强调了 HBV 整合在肿瘤发生中的作用以及了解其对肿瘤生物学影响的必要性。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了非肿瘤和肿瘤肝组织中的 HBV 整合模式,重点关注整合位点的克隆性和多样性。它检查了 HBV 相关 HCC 患者,并将其与非 HBV 相关 HCC 病例进行比较,以评估整合事件与肿瘤抑制基因改变之间的关联。
elements_zh.methods: 基因组 全测序用于识别 HCC 中的复发性整合热点,包括 TERT、KMT2B/MLL4 和 CCNE1。该研究还通过分析 HBx 蛋白的断点和截短,评估了 HBV 整合对肿瘤抑制途径的频率和影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 在高达 79.3% 的 HBV 相关 HCC 病例中检测到 C 端截短的 HBx 蛋白,并且与转移潜力的特征相关。在高达 48% 的 HBV 相关肿瘤中发现了肿瘤抑制基因的改变,包括 突变 和缺失,而在非 HBV 相关的 HCC 中这一比例为 16%。HBV 整合事件与 244 个肿瘤抑制基因的缺失或失活相关,其中包括 TP53 和 RB1。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,HBV 整合通过直接破坏肿瘤抑制基因和增强子介导的癌基因激活而导致肝癌发生。该研究强调了整合相关的结构重排在促进侵袭性肿瘤生物学方面的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果对于改善 HCC 中 HBV 驱动的致癌途径的检测和监测具有重要意义。他们还强调需要进行整合位点分析,以更好地了解 HBV 相关肝癌发生的机制并指导临床决策。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于观察数据,并未建立因果关系。证据是中等的,因为它基于基因组分析和临床观察,没有对 HBV 整合与 HCC 进展之间的因果关系进行实验验证。
