full_text: AbstractIntroductionHepatitis B Virus (HBV) causes a significant global health burden. The HBV core (HBc) protein forms the HBV capsid and has a crucial role in the virus replication cycle. When expressed across different platforms, HBc can self-assemble into HBV-capsid-based virus-like particles (VLPs), with a wide range of applications in both fundamental and pharmaceutical research. Due to their ability to display or crosslink foreign antigens on the surface, HBc VLPs are used as vaccine antigens. However, conventional VLP purification methods face challenges in scalability and achieving high yields. Therefore, investigating the generation and purification process of these VLPs is of high interest.MethodsHBc VLPs composed of three different forms of HBc protein were expressed in E. coli – D (full-length, 183 aa), ΔD163 (C-terminal partially truncated, 163 aa), and ΔD149 (C-terminal fully truncated, 149 aa). Polyethyleneimine precipitation (PEI) was performed for excess nucleic acid reduction, followed by two stages of ammonium sulfate precipitation (AS). For a final purification anion-exchange chromatography (AEX) was performed. Purified HBc VPLs were analyzed for purity and stability by SDS-PAGE, native agarose gel electrophoresis, ELISA, Dynamic light scattering, electron microscopy and host cell protein and DNA and endotoxin assays.ResultsThe single AEX step method resulted in high purity (>85%) and reduced host-cell residues comparable to those detected in a sample produced under good manufacturing practice (GMP) conditions. The HBc VLP variants yielded 5.2 mg, 25.9 mg, and 27.8 mg purified capsids per liter E. coli culture, respectively. Our data showed that all three VLP forms preserved their correct assembly and exhibited minimal aggregation.DiscussionWe successfully designed an HBc-VLP purification technique for the purification of different HBV core antigen particles. The purification resulted in highly pure and little aggregated VLP. This purification method is therefore well-positioned to accelerate studies of HBc VLPs.Keywords: anion exchange chromatography, capsid, HBV, purification, VLP 2.Materials and methodsThe pRSF plasmid backbone was kindly provided by Prof. Dr. Michael Nassal (University of Freiburg, Germany). All HBc variants (D residues 1–183, ΔD163 residues 1–163, ΔD149 residues 1–149) are of genotype D, subtype ayw and were synthesized by GeneArt gene synthesis (ThermoFisher, USA) after codon optimization for expression in E. coli. The respective HBc genes were cloned downstream of the T7 promoter by conventional cloning using PfoI and BshTI restriction sites in the pRSF backbone. The resulting plasmid constructs were sequenced using whole-plasmid sequencing (Eurofins, Luxembourg) to verify the correctness of both the backbone and the inserted sequences.2.1.Expression of HBV capsid particlesE. coli BL21 (DE3) containing the respective pRSF-1b expression plasmids were pre-cultured overnight at 37 °C, constantly shaking at 160 rpm in lysogeny broth (LB) supplemented with kanamycin. On the following day, the pre-culture was added to 1 L terrific broth (TB) medium (Krause et al., 2010) (ThermoFisher, USA) to achieve a starting optical density (OD600nm) of 0.2 of the expression cultures. The cultures were allowed to grow until an OD600nm of 0.8–1.0 was reached. The cultures were then induced with 1 mM isopropyl-1-thio-β-d-galactopyranoside (IPTG; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) overnight for 16 h. The expression cultures were grown at 25 °C with constant shaking at 160 rpm throughout the expression process. After expression, the bacteria were harvested by centrifuging at 5000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The pellets were resuspended in 40 mL lysis buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM AEBSF, HCl) supplemented with 10 μg/mL DNase I. Cell suspension was sonicated 2 × 3 min with 30 s pause in between, at 30% on and 60% amplitude on ice-water using a VS70T probe on a Bandelin Sonopuls HD2200 to ensure complete bacterial lysis. Bacterial debris was removed by centrifugation at 20,000 rpm for 1 h at 4 °C.2.2.Protein precipitation using PEI and ammonium sulfateA 5% (v/v) stock solution of branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) with an average 60,000 MW (Cat. No. 33141.03, Serva, Germany) in 0.5 M Tris buffer (pH 8.0) was added to the supernatant at 4 °C while stirring vigorously to a final concentration of 0.5% (v/v). The mixture was incubated for 30 min at 4 °C, followed by centrifugation (20 min at 25,000 rpm). The supernatant was retained for ammonium sulfate (AS) precipitation.The first AS precipitation was performed at 90% (w/v) saturation at 4 °C. A defined amount of AS (Roth, Germany) was added stepwise to the supernatant while stirring continuously, and the mixture was incubated for 1 h. The solution was centrifuged (30 min at 25,000 rpm), and the resulting pellet was dissolved in Tris-Buffered Saline (TBS; 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) to match the volume of the discarded supernatant. Remaining solid contaminants were removed by centrifugation (20 min at 25,000 rpm), and the supernatant was dialyzed overnight against 2 L of TBS using a 10 kDa cutoff dialysis membrane (Serva, Germany). The contents of the dialysis tube were centrifuged (20 min at 25,000 rpm) and the resulting supernatant subjected to subsequent AS precipitation.The second AS precipitation was carried out at either 40% (w/v) saturation for capsids composed of full-length HBc or 25% (w/v) saturation for the two truncated variants. AS was added stepwise under continuous stirring and incubated for 1 h, followed by centrifugation (30 min at 25,000 rpm). The resulting pellet was resuspended in AEX buffer A (10 mM MES/Tris, pH 6.0) in a volume equivalent to that of the discarded supernatant. After centrifugation (20 min at 25,000 rpm), the supernatant was filtered through a 0.45 μm filter and kept free of air bubbles until further processing. All the centrifugation steps with protein solutions were carried out at 4 °C using a A27-8×50 rotor in a Sorvall Lynx 6,000 centrifuge (Thermo Scientific).2.3.Anion exchange chromatography (AEX)Anion exchange chromatography was performed at room temperature using a 5 mL HiTrap Q HP column (Cytiva, USA) packed with Q SepharoseTM High Performance strong anion exchange resin consisting of quaternary ammonium groups coupled to a cross-linked agarose matrix, with a particle size of approximately 34 μm. The column was connected to the HPLC system (Äkta Purifier 10, Cytiva). The column containing quaternary ammonium groups immobilized on a cross-linked agarose matrix (average particle size approximately 34 μm) functions as a strong anion exchanger. The column was pre-equilibrated with AEX buffer A containing 5% (v/v) AEX buffer B (10 mM MES/Tris, pH 6.0, 1.0 M NaCl). After the sample application, the column was washed with AEX buffer A containing 5% (v/v) AEX buffer B (50 mM NaCl), followed by a linear gradient of 1 column volume (CV) from 5 to 20% (v/v) AEX buffer B (50–200 mM NaCl). Bound HBc proteins were eluted using a linear gradient (10 CVs) from 20 to 80% (v/v) AEX buffer B (200–800 mM NaCl). Fractions were collected at defined intervals and monitored by photodiode-array detectors at 254 and 280 nm. Fractions containing HBc proteins with an A280 above 0.2 and the desired ratio between A260 and A280 (determined using a Peqlab Nanodrop 2000 spectrophotometer, Thermo Scientific) (for HBV D = 1.60–1.70; ∆D163 = 1.10–1.20; ∆D149 = 0.65–0.70), were pooled and subsequently dialyzed against 2 L of storage buffer (PBS containing 6 mM EDTA) to remove excess salts and buffer components. The total soluble protein amounts were determined by the Bradford assay (Bradford, 1976). The purified capsid particles were then stored at 4 °C throughout the study.2.4.Determination of host cell contaminationsResidual E. coli proteins and endotoxin levels in the purified preparation were quantified using the E. coli HCP ELISA kit (Cygnus, USA); limit of detection (LOD) ~ 0.4 ng/mL, lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) ~ 3 ng/mL and PierceTM Chromogenic Endotoxin Quant Kit (Thermo Fisher, USA; LOD and LLOQ 0.01 EU/ml), respectively, following the manufacturer’s instructions. For host cell DNA contamination assessment, total DNA was first extracted from the samples using the NucleoSpin Tissue kit (Macherey-Nagel, Germany). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was then performed on the extracted DNA using the LightCycler 480 system and SYBRTM Green PCR Master Mix, with ER-F3 (GCTCGTGTTGTGAAATGTTG) and ER-R3 (GTAAGGGCCATGATGACTTG) as forward and reverse primers, respectively (Lee et al., 2010).2.5.Sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE)The samples collected during and after the purification process were analyzed by SDS-PAGE using 15% polyacrylamide gels. 10 μL of purified protein samples were denatured by mixing with 2 μL Laemmli SDS buffer, reducing (6x; ThermoFisher, USA), followed by heating at 95 °C for 10 min Samples were then centrifuged briefly at 15,000 rpm for 1 min before loading onto the gel for electrophoresis. SDS-PAGE was conducted with the Mini-PROTEAN Tetra Vertical Electrophoresis Cell (Bio-Rad, USA) system under a constant current of 20 mA per gel. Following electrophoresis, the gels were stained using Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 (Roth, Germany) and analyzed using ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, USA) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. The purity of the final product was assessed using Image Lab 6.1 software (Bio-Rad, USA).2.6.Native agarose gel electrophoresis (NAGE)Native agarose gel electrophoresis was used to analyze capsids in their native form. A 1% agarose (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) gel was prepared in 1x Tris-Acetate Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA; TAE) buffer (40 mM Tris, 5 mM acetate [CH3COONa], and 0.9 mM EDTA, pH 7.9) using the PerfectBlue Mini M Gel System (VWR, USA). Electrophoresis was performed at 110 V for 1 h. Following electrophoresis, gels were sequentially stained with Roti®GelStain (Roth, Germany) to detect encapsulated nucleic acids and Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 (Roth, Germany) to visualize native capsid protein bands. Gel imaging and analysis were performed using the ChemiDoc MP system (Bio-Rad, USA).2.7.Western blot analysisWestern blot analysis was performed following the wet transfer of proteins from polyacrylamide gels or agarose gels onto AmershamTM HybondTM PVDF membrane (0.45 μm; GE Healthcare, USA) using Mini Trans-Blot® Cell (Bio-Rad, USA). Membrane blocking was carried out for 1 h using 5% (w/v) skim milk powder (Roth, Germany) in 1 × Tris-buffered saline (TBS) supplemented with Tween 20 (TBS-T) buffer (20 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, and 0.1% Tween 20, pH 7.6). The primary antibody 8C9-11 (anti-HBc monoclonal antibody, Core Facility Monoclonal Antibodies, Helmholtz Munich) (Ko et al., 2018), diluted 1:1 in blocking buffer, was applied overnight at 4 °C under constant mixing. Membranes were washed three times with TBS-T (50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.6, 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween 20) before incubation with the HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (goat anti-mouse, Sigma-Aldrich, USA). After additional washing, signal detection was performed using an enhanced chemoluminescence (ECL) substrate (Thermo Fisher, USA) and analyzed with the ChemiDoc MP system (Bio-Rad, USA).2.8.In-house sandwich HBcAg enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)The integrity of HBc VLPs was assessed using an in-house ELISA. Microtiter plates were coated with 1 μg/mL anti-HBcAg capture antibody overnight at 4 °C. prior to adding the protein samples, the wells were blocked with 5% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 1 h at room temperature to minimize unspecific binding of the detection antibody. Thereafter, purified protein samples (20 ng/mL) were added to the wells along with a dilution series of BSA standard (ranging from 0 to 50 ng/mL). The samples were prepared in assay diluent (1% BSA/PBS) and incubated for 2 h at room temperature. The captured HBc VLPs were detected by the detection antibody after 1 h of incubation. Both antibodies were kindly provided by the Centro de Ingeniería Genética y Biotecnología de Cuba. Color development was achieved with TMB Single Solution (Life Technologies, USA), and the reaction was stopped by adding 2 M sulfuric acid (Roth, Germany). Absorbance was recorded at 450 nm with a reference wavelength of 560 nm using an Infinite F200 plate reader. Each procedural step was followed by washing with 0.05% PBS-T as indicated.2.9.Dynamic light scattering (DLS)To determine the particle size distribution, DLS was performed on a Zetasizer Nano ZS instrument (Malvern Instruments Ltd., Malvern, UK). 5 μg of HBc VLPs were diluted in 10 mM NaCl and analyzed. The DLS results were analyzed using the DTS software (Malvern, version 6.32).2.10.Transmission electron microscopy (TEM)HBc VLPs were observed under a transmission electron microscope. Continuous carbon grids were glow-discharged for 30 s at 20 mA using GloQube Plus (Quorum, UK). Sample absorption was performed for 1 min before the samples were stained with 2% uranyl acetate solution for 30s. TEM was conducted using JEM-1400Plus (JEOL, Japan) operated at 120 kV, equipped with CCD camera Ruby (JEOL, Japan). Micrographs were taken at a nominal magnification of 60 k with a final pixel size of 2.75 A/px. 3.2.An HBc VLP one-step anion exchange chromatography method produces highly pure and intact HBV capsid particlesProteins expressed in bacterial systems often contain substantial levels of host-derived contaminants (Disela et al., 2024; İncir and Kaplan, 2024). The persistence of contaminating host cell nucleotides poses a major challenge for HBc purification, as the negatively charged nucleic acids in the lysate exhibit a strong affinity for anion-exchange resins. This competitive binding can reduce chromatographic resolution and lower final protein yield. To minimize host nucleic acid contamination, a DNase I treatment was performed during the lysis (Lim et al., 2018), followed by 0.5% (v/v) polyethyleneimine (PEI) precipitation of the supernatant after centrifugation of the lysate (Huber et al., 2019). Collectively, these steps reduced the risk of negatively charged nucleic acids binding to the chromatography column (Burgess, 2009; Stone et al., 2018) and substantially reduced the DNA content in the VLP preparations throughout the purification process.Subsequently, an AS precipitation step (90% (w/v) saturation) was performed, followed by dialysis. This step was primarily aimed at removing the majority of the remaining PEI from the protein solution while retaining the maximum HBc content. To further improve the separation of HBc VLPs from host E. coli proteins, an additional AS precipitation was implemented. For VLPs formed out of truncated HBc proteins (ΔD163, ΔD149), a 25% saturation was applied, resulting in an almost complete precipitation of the HBc proteins. For VLPs formed out of full-length HBc (D) a 25% saturation only partially precipitated the protein. Therefore, the AS concentration was increased to 40%. This improved the yield of HBc proteins but also increased the amount of precipitated host cell proteins (Figures 2B,D,F).Figure 2Representation of purification process HBcAg particles D, ΔD163, ΔD149. The chromatograms (A,C,E) show the characteristic peaks of the eluted HBc VLPs. SDS-PAGEs (B,D,F) show samples of the individual purification steps. 1 = ladder, 2 = bacterial lysate, 3 = PEI precipitation SN, 4 = 90% AS precipitation pellet, 5 = first dialysis, 6 = 40%/25% AS precipitation pellet, 7 = pooled eluates after AEX, 8 = end dialysis to final buffer (PBS, 6 mM EDTA, pH 7.4).Panel A shows a line graph with absorbance (milli-Absorbance Units) on the y-axis and volume (milliliters) on the x-axis, displaying three colored traces for 280 nanometers, 254 nanometers, and conductivity, with an elution peak labeled; salt concentration is also indicated. Panel B contains an SDS-PAGE gel image with eight vertical lanes, each corresponding to a different purification step detailed in the adjacent key, ranging from bacterial lysate to end dialysis, with visible protein bands. Panel C displays another absorbance versus volume chromatogram, and panel D shows an SDS-PAGE gel with eight lanes representing a similar purification sequence with visible protein band patterns. Panel E has a third chromatogram and panel F presents another SDS-PAGE gel, also with eight lanes for corresponding purification steps, each lane showing resolved protein bands of varying intensity.Resuspended pellets from the previous step were then subjected to anion exchange chromatography (AEX) using HiTrap Q HP column (Cytiva, USA) acting as a strong anion exchange resin. During the chromatography process (Figures 2A,C,E), the eluates were continuously monitored for the presence of soluble proteins and nucleic acids. Using the salt gradient, we were able to separate the capsids, as shown in Coomassie-stained gels (Figures 2B,D,F). For full-length D VLPs, the elution peak was defined by a high A254 nm signal that exceeded the A280 nm signal (average (av.) 1.67, Figure 2A). Although only the total nuclease content was measured by A254 nm, the findings were consistent with the presence of internally packaged nucleic acids, as shown later (Figure 3B). For ΔD163, the A254 nm signal was only slightly higher than the A280 nm signal (av. 1.15-fold), reflecting the reduced nucleic acid packaging capacity of these VLP (Figures 2B, 3B). In the case of ΔD149, which exhibits the lowest nucleic acid content among the three variants, the A254 nm signal was notably lower compared to the A280 nm signal (av. 0.67-fold) within the elution peak (Figures 2C, 3B). This could be due to the absence of the nucleic acid-binding CTD, indicating that the eluted particles primarily consisted of empty capsids, which might consequently result in a smaller margin within the A254 nm peak.Figu…

full_text_sections.results: 3.Results3.1.Three different variants of HBc monomers can be efficiently expressed in an inducible bacterial systemVLPs made of varying lengths of HBc were successfully synthesized using pRSF constructs harboring the HBc gene under an inducible T7 promoter. Proteins were expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells carrying the respective plasmid. To minimize the risk of protein aggregation and to favor protein synthesis and VLP assembly, the expression cultures in TB medium were maintained at lower temperatures than the bacteria’s optimal growth temperature (Asor et al., 2020; Hilmer et al., 2008). The expression cultures were initiated at an OD600nm of 0.2 and reached an OD600nm of approx. 1.0 within 4–5 h of growth at 25 °C. At this point, protein expression was induced by adding 1 mM IPTG. The results were then confirmed by WB analysis using the in-house 8C9-11 antibody, which recognizes an N-terminal epitope of HBc. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionIn this study, a method for the purification of HBc VLPs utilizing one AEX chromatography step was demonstrated. Using three different forms of HBc VLPs, we showed that alterations in HBc VLP’s RNA packaging properties, or its absence, influence the efficacy of the downstream purification method. We observed that a C-terminal truncation of HBc can enhance VLP yield and improve purification quality while preserving capsid assembly. Since not every application requires a full-length HBc (Dishlers et al., 2015; Sazegari et al., 2023; Schumacher et al., 2018), our protocol, depending on the specific downstream application, facilitates the efficient purification of HBc variants.After successful expression of all three HBc variants, purification began with key precipitation steps. Purification largely preserved the internally packed RNA, as demonstrated by NAGE (Figure 3B (left)), but excess free nucleic acids were removed by PEI precipitation (Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2011). After the full purification process, only small amounts of residual host-cell DNA were detected, underscoring the effectiveness of PEI. Moreover, it should be noted that in previous protocols that lacked PEI precipitation, the AEX column rapidly overloaded, resulting in inefficient purification. The reason could lie in the negatively charged free nucleic acids binding to the positively charged column, which were now minimized by the precipitation step.Subsequent AS precipitation (90% saturation) and the first dialysis into the AEX buffer were targeted to remove possible PEI residues. In the second AS precipitation step, separating VLPs from host cell proteins yielded the highest yield, with 25% saturation, for particles with truncated HBc proteins. For full-length HBc, we opted for 40% saturation to prevent loss of large quantities of the protein of interest, but at the cost of increased host-cell proteins in the purification preparation (Table 2). Nevertheless, a substantial portion of non-specific host cell proteins could be separated from the HBc VLPs.During chromatography, the elution of HBc VLPs could be precisely monitored by their characteristic peaks. Due to the packed RNA inside the particles, the A254 nm measurement (Figure 2A,C,E) shows a specific peak that even exceeds the peak of the A280 nm measurement for full-length HBc VLPs and stays approximately equal for ΔD163 VLPs. A254 nm signal remains low during the elution for ΔD149 VLPs, indicating the elution of mostly empty capsids (Valentic et al., 2022). Although these observations remain indirect, as total nucleic acids were monitored, they were later supported by nucleic acid staining in NAGE that showed co-localization with HBc VLP bands (Figure 3B).Nevertheless, these findings highlight the distinct nucleic acid binding properties of the three HBc variants. Depending on the intended use of the VLP, this could be exploited during production, as it allows RNA-packed and almost empty particles to be selectively differentiated and sorted during chromatography. The yield of VLPs with truncated HBc was substantially higher than the VLP with full-length HBc containing arginin-rich domain. A similar trend has been observed previously. Factors such as mRNA confirmation and stability, as well as interactions between the C-terminal region of newly synthesized HBc and RNA are hypothesized to contribute to the limited expression of full-length variants (Berza et al., 2013; Sominskaya et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2003). The product recovery of full-length HBc VLPs further demonstrates the increased challenge of purifying the particles composed of full-length HBc by a one-step purification but simultaneously highlights the successful recovery of the particles with truncated HBc (Table 1). On the one hand, this results from the comparably higher loss of protein after each AS precipitation; on the other hand, more nucleic acids may adhere to the outside of full-length proteins or in the purification preparation, resulting in competitive binding to the column and reducing the chromatographic resolution (Valentic et al., 2022). Another reason could be that, in general, proteins adhered more prominently to VLPs containing full-length HBc than to those containing truncated HBc, as indicated by the measured host cell protein and endotoxin levels (Table 2). Overall, the yield of all three VLPs, combined with achieved purities of >85% for D, >90% for ΔD163, and >94% for ΔD149 VLPs, is exceptional compared to similar one-step purification processes (Li et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2018).After purification, host cell protein and endotoxin levels were slightly higher than in a GMP sample used for comparison, but remained low and majorly within the tolerated limits for medical applications, e.g., as vaccine antigens. Endotoxin levels were 78.1 ± 2.1 EU/ml, 70.2 ± 0.4 EU/ml, and 59.5 ± 1.0 EU/ml, normalized to a capsid concentration of 0.1 mg/mL, corresponding to 781 EU/mg, 702 EU/mg, and 595 EU/mg, respectively. Based on the K/M calculation defined in Ph. Eur. 5.1.10, these endotoxin levels would theoretically permit intravenous administration of up to 6.40 μg (D), 7.12 μg (ΔD163), and 8.40 μg (ΔD149) capsid per kg body mass, respectively (EDQM, 2023a, 2023b).For residual host cell protein, no universal acceptance threshold has been established; acceptable levels are instead determined on a product-specific basis. A commonly used benchmark is <100 ng/mg product (100 ppm) (Graham et al., 2026). The measured HCP concentrations of 37.0 ± 21.9 ng/mL (D), 1.2 ± 0.8 ng/mL (ΔD163), and 0.8 ± 0.1 ng/mL (ΔD149), normalized to 0.1 mg/mL capsid, correspond to 370 ng/mg, 12 ng/mg, and 8 ng/mg capsid, respectively. Thus, the latter two variants were below the commonly used benchmark, whereas the first remained above it.Thus, the longer the HBc protein of which the VLP was formed, the more host cell residues were detected in the sample. The reasons remain uncertain, as other literature supports a similar trend for associated host nucleic acids, but a contradictory tendency for host cell proteins (Pusara et al., 2024; Sominskaya et al., 2013). Stability tests after purification showed that the capsid structure of the VLPs remained intact and correctly assembled over an extended period when stored in PBS containing 6 mM EDTA at 4 °C without obvious aggregation.Taken together, we established a single-step chromatography purification method for HBc VLPs that can be broadly applied for different HBc variants, does not require specific lab equipment, and generates VLPs of high quality that can be stored at 4 °C.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionChronic hepatitis B, caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), is a major global health concern. It affects more than 240 million individuals worldwide and resulted in approximately 1.1 million deaths in 2024 (WHO, 2026). Current standard treatments using nucleos(t)ide analogs rarely achieve a functional cure in infected individuals (Gehring and Protzer, 2019). The covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), the persistent form of HBV in the nucleus of an infected cell, poses a daunting challenge, making it difficult to cure the infection with current therapeutic strategies. Failure to eliminate cccDNA may result in viral reactivation upon cessation of medication (Lucifora and Protzer, 2016; Revill et al., 2016). This requires long-term treatment, underscoring the critical need for novel, curative therapeutic strategies.The HBV core protein (HBc) is the only component of the HBV capsid and plays a pivotal role at various stages of viral replication (Zlotnick et al., 2015). The viral capsid encapsidates the pregenomic RNA (pgRNA) of HBV and serves as the site for reverse transcription and formation of the HBV DNA genome (Shen et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2015). The HBc monomer is a 21 kDa protein composed of 183 amino acids, with the first 149 aa forming the assembly domain and aa 150 to 183 constituting the arginine-rich C-terminal domain (CTD) responsible for nucleic acid binding (Birnbaum and Nassal, 1990). Following their dimerization, HBc dimers can spontaneously self-assemble into icosahedral capsids of either T = 3 or T = 4 symmetry, comprising 90 or 120 dimers, respectively (Alom et al., 2024; Selzer and Zlotnick, 2015). Truncations in the CTD up to residue 149 have been reported to enhance bacterial expression levels and result in a predominance of T = 4 capsids, without causing any noticeable alterations in particle morphology (Wang et al., 2019). This adaptability renders recombinant HBV capsids an important platform for investigating viral assembly mechanisms but also enables the development of virus-like particles (VLPs) for diverse biomedical applications.Prior reports have demonstrated that HBc-based VLPs expressed in bacterial systems are well suited for a range of biological applications (Hassebroek et al., 2023; Petrovskis et al., 2021). Leveraging their immunogenic properties, HBc VLPs have been used to develop therapeutic vaccines for chronic hepatitis B (Backes et al., 2016; Buchmann et al., 2013; Su et al., 2024). Owing to their unique structural characteristics and ability to self-assemble, HBc VLPs have also emerged as a versatile platform for presenting foreign antigens, expanding their use as a vaccine platform (Dishlers et al., 2023; Fatema et al., 2025; Moradi Vahdat et al., 2021). Beyond these applications, HBc VLPs can also be engineered for the targeted delivery of therapeutic agents or adjuvants (Mohamed Suffian et al., 2017; Sacherl et al., 2023). Additionally, purified HBc VLPs are valuable for screening antiviral compounds, such as capsid assembly modulators (Burdette et al., 2023), and for structural and mechanistic studies (Lecoq et al., 2023) aimed at an in-depth understanding of virion assembly and HBV pathogenesis. Given such diverse applications, the need for more efficient production methods and rapid purification protocols to obtain highly pure HBV capsid particle variants is steadily growing.A widely used conventional method at the laboratory level for purifying HBc VLPs is sucrose density gradient centrifugation (Chevreuil et al., 2020; Fatema et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2023). Additionally, various chromatography techniques, such as ion exchange chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), have been employed to purify HBc VLPs (Berke et al., 2017; Petrovskis et al., 2021; Selzer et al., 2014). However, these methods often require combining multiple approaches and several steps to achieve high purity. On the other hand, more selective methods, such as affinity chromatography, can achieve high purity; however, they often yield lower amounts and may require the addition of a tag. This can limit their applicability and potentially interfere with downstream applications (Bin Mohamed Suffian et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2023). As previously reported, two consecutive SEC steps are commonly used to purify HBc VLPs, resulting in broad elution peaks that make separation of host cell proteins and the VLPs difficult (Orabi et al., 2015). Adapting the protocol to two anion-exchange chromatography (AEX) largely reduced the yield. As HBc VLPs are known to associate with host RNAs (Porterfield et al., 2010), we introduced a polyethyleneimine (PEI) precipitation step to remove excess surface-associated host nucleic acids that are not encapsulated within the capsids, thereby eliminating the need for a second AEX run. Here, we present a one-step ion-exchange chromatography method for purifying three variants of HBc VLPs. These variants were derived from C-terminal truncations of the HBV genotype D HBc protein, namely, the full-length HBc (D), semi-truncated HBc (ΔD163), and truncated HBc (ΔD149), with the latter exhibiting a complete absence of the nucleic acid-binding CTD. All three capsid variants were successfully purified to comparable purity levels. 2.1.Expression of HBV capsid particlesE. coli BL21 (DE3) containing the respective pRSF-1b expression plasmids were pre-cultured overnight at 37 °C, constantly shaking at 160 rpm in lysogeny broth (LB) supplemented with kanamycin. On the following day, the pre-culture was added to 1 L terrific broth (TB) medium (Krause et al., 2010) (ThermoFisher, USA) to achieve a starting optical density (OD600nm) of 0.2 of the expression cultures. The cultures were allowed to grow until an OD600nm of 0.8–1.0 was reached. The cultures were then induced with 1 mM isopropyl-1-thio-β-d-galactopyranoside (IPTG; Sigma-Aldrich, USA) overnight for 16 h. The expression cultures were grown at 25 °C with constant shaking at 160 rpm throughout the expression process. After expression, the bacteria were harvested by centrifuging at 5000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The pellets were resuspended in 40 mL lysis buffer (50 mM Tris–HCl pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM AEBSF, HCl) supplemented with 10 μg/mL DNase I. Cell suspension was sonicated 2 × 3 min with 30 s pause in between, at 30% on and 60% amplitude on ice-water using a VS70T probe on a Bandelin Sonopuls HD2200 to ensure complete bacterial lysis. Bacterial debris was removed by centrifugation at 20,000 rpm for 1 h at 4 °C. 2.2.Protein precipitation using PEI and ammonium sulfateA 5% (v/v) stock solution of branched polyethyleneimine (PEI) with an average 60,000 MW (Cat. The mixture was incubated for 30 min at 4 °C, followed by centrifugation (20 min at 25,000 rpm). The supernatant was retained for ammonium sulfate (AS) precipitation.The first AS precipitation was performed at 90% (w/v) saturation at 4 °C. The solution was centrifuged (30 min at 25,000 rpm), and the resulting pellet was dissolved in Tris-Buffered Saline (TBS; 50 mM Tris–HCl, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl) to match the volume of the discarded supernatant. full_text: Abstract Background Chronic viral hepatitis due to hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) remains a significant global public health problem and a leading cause of liver-related morbidity and mortality, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. In Nigeria, including Nasarawa State, a substantial burden persists; however, data on prevalence and associated risk factors across community- and facility-based populations remain limited. This study assessed the prevalence of HBV and HCV infections and identified associated risk factors among adults in community-based (Lafia and Akwanga) and facility-based (Keffi) populations in Nasarawa State, Nigeria. Methods A cross-sectional analytical study was conducted among 852 adults recruited from three distinct study settings in Nasarawa State, North-Central Nigeria: a tertiary healthcare facility population at the Federal Medical Centre, Keffi, and two community-based populations in Akwanga and Lafia Local Government Areas (284 participants per study setting). Socio-demographic, behavioural, healthcare-related, and household exposure data were collected using structured questionnaires. Participants were screened using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), followed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which served as the reference standard for infection classification. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0, applying descriptive statistics, bivariate analysis (crude odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals), and multivariable logistic regression (adjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals), with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Prevalence estimates were disaggregated by study setting (community-based versus facility-based populations). Results The overall PCR-confirmed prevalence of HBV was 12.91% (community: 11.80%; facility: 15.14%), while HCV prevalence was 7.04% (community: 5.28%; facility: 10.56%). No statistically significant difference was observed in HBV prevalence between community and facility populations (χ2 = 1.86; p = 0.206), whereas HCV prevalence was significantly higher among facility-based participants (χ2 = 7.028; p = 0.007). Factors independently associated with HBV infection included sharing of personal hygiene items (AOR = 1.73; 95% CI: 1.06–2.70; p = 0.040) and history of sexually transmitted infections (AOR = 2.47; 95% CI: 1.38–4.42; p = 0.030). For HCV, history of blood transfusion was independently associated with infection (AOR = 2.11; 95% CI: 1.04–4.31; p = 0.040). Conclusion HBV and HCV infections remain prevalent in both community- and facility-based populations in Nasarawa State. The identified behavioural and healthcare-related exposures are associated with infection, highlighting the need for expanded vaccination programmes, routine hepatitis screening, community education, strengthened infection prevention and control measures. Targeted, context-specific public health interventions are required to support prevention, early detection, and management of viral hepatitis and contribute to Nigeria’s 2030 viral hepatitis elimination goals. full_text: SUMMARYHepatitis B is a common vaccine-preventable and treatable condition. Chronic hepatitis B is often asymptomatic and can be missed if the diagnosis is not actively considered.The World Health Organization and the Australian Government have committed to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat by 2030. The tools required to achieve this are available: an effective vaccine, accurate blood tests for diagnosis and monitoring, effective antiviral treatments and access to ultrasound to enable early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma.Risk-based testing approaches are not effective enough to enable Australia to achieve elimination targets; hence, the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025–2030 calls for population-wide testing to identify hepatitis B status.Chronic hepatitis B is a lifelong disease that requires long-term monitoring and follow-up irrespective of the stage of disease or whether an individual is taking antiviral treatment.Most healthcare for people living with chronic hepatitis B can be provided in primary care. All medical practitioners and authorised nurse practitioners can now prescribe antiviral therapy for hepatitis B; additional accreditation is no longer required.Holistic care includes the provision of resources in a person’s preferred language, peer and cultural support workers, access to a long-term effective model of care, and appropriate monitoring. Continuity of healthcare providers is desirable and an important enabler of sustained engagement in care. ConclusionPeople living with CHB experience significant morbidity and mortality, which can be prevented and managed within an already publicly funded toolkit of vaccination, testing, diagnosis, management and treatment options. Removing the barriers to accessing this care is an urgent priority if Australia is going to meet the elimination targets it has committed to. The foundation step is for everyone to know their hepatitis B status through universal testing; only then can holistic care be provided to those who are living with CHB through decentralised models of care tailored to community and culture. IntroductionOne-third of the world’s population has been exposed to hepatitis B, with an estimated 254 million people currently living with chronic hepatitis B (CHB).1 An estimated 227,000 people are living with CHB in Australia.2The hepatitis B virus is the second most potent carcinogen after tobacco,3 increasing the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) by its very presence. Therefore, unlike other causes of hepatitis, such as hepatitis C, where significant liver fibrosis or cirrhosis needs to be present before HCC risk increases, people living with CHB have an increased risk of HCC irrespective of their cirrhotic status. CHB causes inflammation of the liver that can progress to cirrhosis and HCC. One-quarter of people with untreated CHB will die from either HCC or liver failure.4 Although treatment does not cure the infection, it can prevent progression to cirrhosis and reduces the risk of HCC.In 2016, the World Health Assembly committed to the elimination of hepatitis B as a major public health threat by 2030, and an elimination strategy was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO).5 Australia’s ongoing commitment to this elimination goal is reiterated in the Fourth National Hepatitis B Strategy 2025–2030.6Despite having all the necessary tools to eliminate hepatitis B as a public health threat, it is estimated that in Australia, 1 in 3 of the 227,000 people living with CHB are not aware of their diagnosis and only 1 in 4 are receiving guideline-based care. In addition, only small increases in the uptake of antiviral treatment have been seen over the past decade.2 Many barriers to accessing testing, diagnosis and care exist, including (but not limited to) the asymptomatic nature of CHB, a lack of knowledge and understanding of risk factors, stigma, remoteness, the logistics of accessing care through tertiary services, English commonly not being a patient’s first language and systematic consequences of a CHB diagnosis, particularly in the immigration system.Elimination requires a paradigm shift in the care provided to people living with CHB to increase:hepatitis B testing through population-wide universal offer of testing, treatment, enabling earlier diagnosisprimary care provision of hepatitis B testing, follow-up and long-term monitoring of those living with CHBthe number of people on treatment.Any changes in the approach to hepatitis B management need to be developed in consultation with affected individuals and communities to ensure stigma and discrimination are addressed and to minimise the personal and social impacts of hepatitis B.7Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia are disproportionately impacted by CHB, with an overall prevalence of 3.4%, compared with 0.8% for Australia as a whole, increasing to more than 6% in some regions.8 Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory have a unique subgenotype of hepatitis B virus (HBV/C4) that has genotypic and phenotypic markers of faster progression to cirrhosis and increased risk of HCC, which further increases the urgency for early diagnosis and engagement in care. Some people born overseas are also at higher risk of CHB for many different reasons, predominantly influenced by the prevalence of CHB in the country they were born in and the availability of a hepatitis vaccine as part of the infant vaccine schedule in that country.This article aims to provide an update and guidance for healthcare professionals across Australia to play their part in the elimination of CHB. Diagnosis: towards universal testing of all adultsPeople living with CHB are often asymptomatic and may have normal liver function tests, so an active case-finding approach is needed. full_text: BackgroundCHB remains a major public health burden in China. TikTok, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu have become key channels for health information, yet the quality, reliability, and transparency of such content remain uncertain.MethodsOn November 12, 2025, the top 100 eligible HBV-related videos from each platform (N = 300) were assessed using the Global Quality Scale (GQS), modified DISCERN instrument (mDISCERN), and Journal of the American Medical Association benchmark criteria (JAMA). Two raters independently scored each video; discrepant ratings were resolved by consensus or senior adjudication, and final consensus scores were used for the main analyses. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using linearly weighted Cohen's κ. Group differences were evaluated using the Kruskal–Wallis H test followed, when significant, by Dunn's post hoc test with Holm adjustment. Spearman correlations and multivariable ordinal regression models were used to examine unadjusted and adjusted associations.ResultsA total of 300 videos were included, with 100 from each platform. Inter-rater agreement was substantial for GQS (κ = 0.774, 95% CI 0.705–0.839), almost perfect for mDISCERN (κ = 0.928, 95% CI 0.888-0.962), and moderate for JAMA (κ = 0.503, 95% CI 0.410-0.590). mDISCERN and JAMA scores differed significantly across platforms, whereas GQS scores did not. Medical personnel had higher rank distributions than normal users for GQS, mDISCERN, and JAMA after Holm adjustment. In adjusted models, Xiaohongshu was associated with higher GQS scores than Bilibili, normal-user uploaders were associated with lower GQS scores than medical personnel, and longer video duration was associated with higher GQS scores. JAMA showed threshold-specific associations with platform, uploader type, and video duration. The adjusted cumulative mDISCERN model was not formally interpreted because of sparse-data instability; a bias-reduced adjacent-category model was reported as an exploratory sensitivity analysis. Engagement metrics showed weak and inconsistent correlations with quality scores.ConclusionsAmong highly visible hepatitis B-related short videos retrieved under prespecified search conditions, video quality varied by assessment instrument, platform, and uploader type. Adjusted associations were instrument- or threshold-specific, and engagement metrics should not be treated as proxies for reliability or transparency. 2Methods2.1Ethical considerationsThis study analyzed publicly available short-video content and publicly accessible account-level information from Xiaohongshu, Bilibili, and TikTok. The researchers did not interact with users or access private, sensitive, or non-public data. Identifiable account names and video URLs are not reported in this manuscript. Because the study was limited to publicly available online content and did not involve interaction with users or access to private data, no additional informed consent was required.2.2Search strategy and data collectionTo reduce but not eliminate the influence of personalized recommendation algorithms, new accounts with no prior search or viewing history were created for each platform before data collection. Searches were conducted on Xiaohongshu, TikTok, and Bilibili on November 12, 2025, and all searches were completed within 4 h. Two Chinese search terms were used separately on each platform: “乙型肝炎” (“hepatitis B”) and “乙型病毒性肝炎” (“viral hepatitis B”). Search results were reviewed according to the default ranking provided by each platform because highly ranked videos are more likely to represent the information encountered by normal users.For Xiaohongshu and TikTok, the first 200 ranked search results were reviewed sequentially, and the first 100 videos meeting the prespecified eligibility criteria were retained. Screening stopped once the target sample of 100 eligible videos per platform had been reached. At the time of data collection, 100 Bilibili videos were retrieved and retained. These videos were subsequently verified against the same eligibility criteria, and all were confirmed to be eligible. The final sample comprised 300 videos, with 100 videos from each platform.Videos were excluded if they were unrelated to hepatitis B, duplicated within or between the two search results, primarily commercial advertisements, or uploaded within 7 days before the search date. When the same video appeared in the results for both search terms, it was retained only once. A total of 300 videos were included, comprising 100 videos from each platform (Figure 1).Figure 1Platform-specific video identification and selection process.Flowchart illustrating video identification and selection across three platforms: Xiaohongshu and TikTok each began with 200 videos, retaining the first 100 meeting eligibility criteria; Bilibili began with 100 videos, all of which met criteria. Final analysis included 100 videos per platform, totaling 300.Search results were ordered using each platform's default ranking system. The exact weighting of textual relevance, recency, engagement, uploader characteristics, geographic location, device or network information, and other ranking signals was not publicly available and could not be standardized across platforms. Creating new accounts reduced personalization based on prior viewing and search histories, but it could not eliminate cold-start recommendations, platform-specific ranking rules, temporal variation, geographic effects, or possible nondeterministic variation in search results. The retrieved videos should therefore be interpreted as a cross-sectional sample of highly visible results returned under the prespecified search conditions, rather than as a probability sample or exhaustive representation of all hepatitis B-related videos available on each platform.2.3Data extraction and classificationThe following information was extracted for each video on the search date: platform, video URL, uploader identity, number of likes, collections, comments, and shares, uploader follower count, video duration, upload date, and days since upload. Likes, collections, comments, and shares were defined as user engagement indicators. Follower count was treated as an uploader-level characteristic, whereas video duration and days since upload were treated as structural video characteristics. The platform-specific save or favorite function was harmonized as “collections” for cross-platform analysis. All engagement data were recorded on the same date to reduce variation caused by the continuous accumulation of user interactions.Uploader identity was classified into four mutually exclusive categories according to the account profile, platform verification information, and stated institutional affiliation:Medical personnel: individual accounts identified as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, or other licensed or verifiable healthcare professionals;Normal users: individual accounts without a verifiable healthcare professional identity or official medical institutional affiliation, including patients, caregivers, and members of the general public;Medical institutions: official accounts operated by hospitals, clinics, public health institutions, or other healthcare facilities; andOther organizations: accounts operated by nonmedical organizations, media organizations, nonprofit organizations, social organizations, or commercial enterprises.When uploader identity was unclear, the account profile and platform verification information were jointly reviewed by the two evaluators, and disagreements were resolved through discussion with the senior evaluator.Video content was coded using five non-mutually exclusive topic categories:Symptoms: clinical manifestations, signs, or symptoms associated with HBV infection;Causes: HBV etiology, transmission routes, risk factors, and mechanisms of infection;Prevention: vaccination, screening, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infection-control measures, and other preventive behaviors;Treatment: antiviral treatment, treatment indications, medication use, clinical monitoring, and disease management; andPrognosis: disease progression, long-term outcomes, complications, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.Each topic was coded independently as present or absent. A single video could be assigned to more than one topic; therefore, the percentages across the five topic categories did not necessarily sum to 100%.2.4Assessment of video content and qualityEach video was independently assessed by two clinical experts using the GQS, mDISCERN, and JAMA benchmark criteria. Identical ratings were directly retained as the final score. Discrepant ratings were reviewed by the two raters to reach consensus; unresolved discrepancies were adjudicated by a senior reviewer. All three evaluators were frontline clinicians from tertiary hospitals, each with more than 13 years of clinical experience. The final consensus scores were used in the main analyses, whereas the original independent ratings were retained for assessment of inter-rater agreement.The GQS is a 5-point scale used to evaluate the overall educational quality, flow, usefulness, and comprehensiveness of health information, with scores ranging from 1 to 5 (17). The mDISCERN was based on the original DISCERN framework and on the five-item modified DISCERN approach used for evaluating online medical videos, which assesses clarity of aims, reliability of sources, balance and bias, provision of additional sources, and acknowledgement of uncertainty (18, 19). The JAMA benchmark criteria include four items: authorship, attribution, disclosure, and currency; each item is scored as 1 for yes and 0 for no, giving a total score ranging from 0 to 4 (20). Higher scores indicate better quality, reliability, or transparency according to the corresponding instrument. Detailed items and scoring criteria are provided in Supplementary Table S1.2.5Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized as medians and interquartile ranges because of their non-normal distributions. Inter-rater agreement for the ordinal total scores was assessed using linearly weighted Cohen's κ, calculated for the overall sample and separately for each platform. Exact agreement was also reported. The 95% confidence intervals for κ were estimated using 5,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples; overall bootstrap resampling was stratified by platform. Continuous video characteristics and engagement indicators were compared across the three platforms using the Kruskal–Wallis H test because of their non-normal distributions. Binary video-topic indicators were compared across platforms using Pearson's chi-square test. All tests were two-sided. Differences in the final consensus GQS, mDISCERN, and JAMA scores across uploader types, platforms, and presentation formats were assessed using the Kruskal–Wallis H test. When the overall Kruskal–Wallis test was statistically significant, Dunn's post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed, with P values adjusted using the Holm method within each grouping-variable and assessment-instrument combination. Epsilon-squared values were calculated as effect-size estimates for the Kruskal–Wallis tests. Spearman rank correlation analyses were used to examine unadjusted associations between final consensus quality scores and likes, collections, comments, shares, video duration, days since upload, and follower count. Correlations were calculated using pairwise complete observations and were not interpreted as evidence of independent prediction or causality. Separate multivariable ordinal regression models were fitted for the final consensus GQS, mDISCERN, and JAMA scores. Core models included platform, uploader type, follower count, video duration, and days since upload. Follower count, video duration, and days since upload were transformed using log2(x + 1), so the corresponding odds ratios represented the approximate change associated with a doubling of each variable. Bilibili and medical personnel served as reference categories. For GQS and JAMA, predictors satisfying the proportional-odds assumption were modeled using common effects, whereas predictors with non-proportional effects were allowed to vary across cumulative score thresholds in partial proportional-odds cumulative logit models. For mDISCERN, uploader type violated the proportional-odds assumption, and a stable cumulative partial proportional-odds model could not be obtained because of sparse observations in some uploader and score-category combinations. A mean bias-reduced adjacent-category ordinal logistic regression was therefore conducted as an exploratory sensitivity analysis. Extended models additionally adjusted for five video-topic indicators: symptoms, cause, prevention, treatment, and prognosis. Models were evaluated for convergence, coefficient finiteness, covariance or Hessian stability, multicollinearity, and sparse-data problems. All tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 4.4Uploader type, professional expertise, and patient experienceVideos uploaded by medical personnel had higher rank distributions than those uploaded by normal users for all three instruments in the present study. Previous short-video studies have reported source-dependent differences in information quality. Some studies observed higher quality or reliability among professionally produced content, whereas others found no consistent advantage across all instruments or health topics (13–15).The observed uploader-type pattern is plausible in the context of HBV care. Medical personnel are more likely to be familiar with transmission routes, serological testing, HBV DNA interpretation, antiviral-treatment criteria, long-term monitoring, cirrhosis and liver cancer risk, and pregnancy-related prevention (1, 27–29). Nevertheless, professional identity does not automatically guarantee complete source citation, disclosure, or updating, which may help explain why associations differed across instruments and why JAMA effects were threshold-specific.The higher quality-rank distributions observed for medical personnel should not be interpreted as evidence that professional identity alone guarantees reliable communication. Medical credentials confer symbolic and epistemic authority, which may increase perceived credibility and persuasiveness, although evidence regarding sharing behavior remains inconsistent (30, 31). This authority can improve public communication when accompanied by evidence-based explanation, but it may also magnify the consequences of incomplete source attribution, insufficient acknowledgement of uncertainty, unbalanced treatment discussion, outdated guidance, or undisclosed commercial interests (32, 33). Professional status should therefore increase accountability rather than exempt content from scrutiny. The relevant policy distinction is not simply between professional and nonprofessional uploaders, but between credential verification and content-level quality assurance.Normal-user videos may offer lived-experience narratives that differ from professional educational content; however, this potential function was not assessed in the present study (25). Online illness narratives can provide social, emotional, and practical context for patients, but their relevance and applicability may vary across individuals (34, 35). They should therefore be viewed as complementary to, rather than substitutes for, individualized clinical guidance (35). For hepatitis B, a single personal treatment trajectory may not apply to viewers with different viral loads, fibrosis stages, pregnancy status, comorbidities, or treatment histories (1, 27–29). The very small number of videos from other organizations also limits interpretation of that uploader category. 3Results3.1Video characteristicsA total of 300 hepatitis B-related short videos were included, with 100 videos from each platform: Bilibili, TikTok, and Xiaohongshu. Basic video characteristics and engagement indicators differed significantly across platforms (all P < 0.05). TikTok showed the highest user engagement. full_text_sections.discussion: 4Discussion4.1Principal findingsThis study showed that the apparent quality of hepatitis B-related short videos depended on both the assessment instrument and the source of the content. Platform differences were evident for reliability and transparency, as measured by mDISCERN and JAMA, but not for the unadjusted overall GQS comparison. Differences between medical personnel and normal users were observed across all three instruments in the post hoc analyses, whereas the adjusted associations varied by outcome and score threshold. Engagement metrics were only weakly and inconsistently correlated with quality.The divergence between the instruments is clinically relevant rather than contradictory. GQS mainly reflects overall quality, flow, comprehensiveness, and usefulness; mDISCERN emphasizes clarity of aims, reliability of sources, balance and bias, additional sources, and acknowledgement of uncertainty; and JAMA focuses on authorship, attribution, disclosure, and currency (17–20). A short video may be easy to understand and well organized, thereby receiving a favorable GQS score, while still omitting source attribution, uncertainty, disclosure, or updating information required by mDISCERN and JAMA. This distinction helps explain why platform differences were detected for mDISCERN and JAMA but not for the overall unadjusted GQS comparison. It also indicates that comprehensibility, evidence reliability, and transparency are separate quality dimensions that should not be collapsed into a single judgment.4.2Platform algorithms, visibility, and instrument-specific platform differencesThe use of newly created accounts reduced history-based personalization, but it did not make search retrieval algorithmically neutral. Short-video platforms use proprietary ranking and recommendation systems, and public-health research on TikTok and social media has emphasized the need to examine how platform design and recommendation dynamics shape exposure to health content (21, 22). In this study, the sample should therefore be understood as a snapshot of highly visible videos returned under a specific date, keyword, account-status, and default-ranking condition. Algorithm-related selection could have overrepresented or underrepresented particular uploader types, topics, upload dates, engagement profiles, or quality levels, but the direction and magnitude of this potential bias could not be quantified.In the present study, mDISCERN and JAMA scores differed across platforms, whereas the overall unadjusted GQS comparison was not significant. Previous studies of short-video health information have reported platform- or source-dependent differences in information quality, but the direction and consistency of these differences vary across diseases, platforms, and assessment instruments (13–15).The platform-specific findings may partly reflect differences in content ecology, uploader composition, video length, verification practices, and conventions for displaying authorship and source information. These mechanisms were not directly assessed in the present study and remain plausible explanations rather than demonstrated causes. Because JAMA rewards authorship, attribution, disclosure, and currency (20), platform differences in the visibility of such elements could influence transparency scores even when overall educational flow appears similar.The higher unadjusted mDISCERN rank distributions on Xiaohongshu raise an important question about the relationship between experiential narratives and epistemic authority. Conventional credibility models often privilege formal institutional affiliation and professional credentials (23), but online patient and lifestyle-oriented narratives may contribute situated knowledge by describing how illness, treatment, stigma, uncertainty, and self-management are experienced in everyday life (24–26). Such experiential knowledge may improve relevance and contextual understanding, but it does not replace clinical evidence or establish factual accuracy. The degree of experiential narration was not directly coded in this study, and the adjusted cumulative mDISCERN model was not formally interpreted; therefore, this explanation should be treated as a plausible interpretation rather than a demonstrated mechanism.Because mDISCERN rewards explicit aims, source cues, balance, additional resources, and acknowledgement of uncertainty, a conversational or experiential format could theoretically perform well when creators clearly delimit personal experience, distinguish it from general medical advice, and provide supporting sources. This possibility was not directly tested in the present study.The absence of a significant unadjusted platform difference for GQS and the adjusted association between Xiaohongshu and higher GQS scores should be interpreted as answering different questions rather than as conflicting results. The Kruskal–Wallis test compared overall unadjusted rank distributions across platforms, whereas the ordinal regression model adjusted for uploader type, follower count, video duration, and days since upload. One plausible explanation is that additional duration provides more space for structured and comprehensive explanations, although this mechanism was not directly examined in the present study. Longer videos do not necessarily improve authorship disclosure, source attribution, conflict disclosure, or currency, because these transparency elements are separate from narrative length.4.3Why hepatitis B information is difficult to compress into short videosHepatitis B presents a public health communication challenge that is distinct from many acute or symptom-driven conditions. Chronic HBV infection can remain clinically silent for years, and treatment decisions cannot be made on symptoms alone (2, 27–29). Appropriate management requires laboratory-based staging and longitudinal evaluation, including HBsAg testing, HBV DNA assessment, liver function tests, fibrosis assessment, antiviral-treatment eligibility, adherence to long-term therapy, monitoring during treatment, and surveillance for cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (1, 27–29). These multi-step decisions are difficult to communicate fully in very short videos, especially when content is simplified into binary messages such as positive versus negative, symptomatic versus asymptomatic, or medication versus no medication.This complexity means that incomplete online explanations may have consequences beyond general health literacy. A video that encourages testing or vaccination may be beneficial, but advice about treatment eligibility, medication discontinuation, pregnancy management, or liver cancer surveillance requires careful qualification (1, 27–29). In a condition characterized by gaps between infection, diagnosis, linkage to care, and treatment, simplified messages could potentially reinforce misunderstandings such as the belief that absence of symptoms means no need for testing, that normal liver function eliminates the need for follow-up, that short-term medication can be stopped independently, or that all HBsAg-positive individuals require immediate treatment. These examples are public health concerns relevant to hepatitis B communication; they were not directly measured as misinformation events in the present sample.4.4Uploader type, professional expertise, and patient experienceVideos uploaded by medical personnel had higher rank distributions than those uploaded by normal users for all three instruments in the present study. Previous short-video studies have reported source-dependent differences in information quality. Some studies observed higher quality or reliability among professionally produced content, whereas others found no consistent advantage across all instruments or health topics (13–15).The observed uploader-type pattern is plausible in the context of HBV care. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAmong highly visible hepatitis B-related short videos retrieved under the prespecified search conditions, quality varied according to the assessment instrument, platform, and uploader type. Platform differences were observed for mDISCERN and JAMA but not for the overall GQS comparison, while videos uploaded by medical personnel had higher rank distributions across the three instruments than videos uploaded by normal users. Adjusted associations were instrument- and threshold-specific, including patterns involving Xiaohongshu, normal-user uploaders, video duration, and follower count, indicating that no single platform or uploader characteristic was consistently associated with all dimensions of video quality. Engagement metrics were only weakly and inconsistently related to quality and should not be used as proxies for reliability or transparency. These findings support platform-specific quality improvement that emphasizes professional accountability, content-level review, source attribution, information currency, and evidence-based hepatitis B guidance.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionChronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global and Chinese public health burden. HBV can cause chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, and many infected people remain undiagnosed or are not linked to appropriate care (1, 2). Recent epidemiological evidence indicates that China still has a substantial burden of chronic HBV infection, although prevalence has changed over time with vaccination and prevention efforts (3, 4).Digital media and short-video platforms have become important channels for health information seeking and public health communication. Social media can expand the reach of health messages (5), and TikTok has been identified as a source from which users obtain health information and misinformation (6). However, objective assessments and reviews of health-related short videos have shown that accessibility and popularity do not necessarily ensure scientific reliability or transparency (7–9). These concerns are particularly relevant for HBV because prevention, testing, treatment eligibility, and long-term monitoring require medically accurate explanations.Previous research has documented broader risks related to health misinformation and infodemics online (10, 11). At the same time, social media-based interventions have been used to promote HBV screening and liver cancer prevention in specific communities (12). Studies evaluating short videos on other health topics have reported variable quality and reliability across platforms and diseases (13–15). However, evidence remains limited on HBV-related short videos across multiple Chinese-language platforms, and other-disease findings cannot be assumed to apply directly to HBV.Bilibili's 2024 annual report describes the platform as a video community with a strong content ecosystem and knowledge-sharing functions (16). This platform background supports the rationale for cross-platform comparison, but it should not be interpreted as evidence that any platform produces higher-quality medical information.Therefore, this study quantitatively evaluated the content characteristics, scientific quality, and reliability of HBV-related short videos on TikTok, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu. We also examined the relationship between video quality and user engagement. These findings may provide evidence for improving HBV-related health communication on social media and strengthening public awareness of HBV prevention and control. 2.1Ethical considerationsThis study analyzed publicly available short-video content and publicly accessible account-level information from Xiaohongshu, Bilibili, and TikTok. The researchers did not interact with users or access private, sensitive, or non-public data. Identifiable account names and video URLs are not reported in this manuscript. Because the study was limited to publicly available online content and did not involve interaction with users or access to private data, no additional informed consent was required. 2.2Search strategy and data collectionTo reduce but not eliminate the influence of personalized recommendation algorithms, new accounts with no prior search or viewing history were created for each platform before data collection. Searches were conducted on Xiaohongshu, TikTok, and Bilibili on November 12, 2025, and all searches were completed within 4 h. Two Chinese search terms were used separately on each platform: “乙型肝炎” (“hepatitis B”) and “乙型病毒性肝炎” (“viral hepatitis B”). Search results were reviewed according to the default ranking provided by each platform because highly ranked videos are more likely to represent the information encountered by normal users.For Xiaohongshu and TikTok, the first 200 ranked search results were reviewed sequentially, and the first 100 videos meeting the prespecified eligibility criteria were retained. Screening stopped once the target sample of 100 eligible videos per platform had been reached. At the time of data collection, 100 Bilibili videos were retrieved and retained. These videos were subsequently verified against the same eligibility criteria, and all were confirmed to be eligible. The final sample comprised 300 videos, with 100 videos from each platform.Videos were excluded if they were unrelated to hepatitis B, duplicated within or between the two search results, primarily commercial advertisements, or uploaded within 7 days before the search date. When the same video appeared in the results for both search terms, it was retained only once. A total of 300 videos were included, comprising 100 videos from each platform (Figure 1).Figure 1Platform-specific video identification and selection process.Flowchart illustrating video identification and selection across three platforms: Xiaohongshu and TikTok each began with 200 videos, retaining the first 100 meeting eligibility criteria; Bilibili began with 100 videos, all of which met criteria. Final analysis included 100 videos per platform, totaling 300.Search results were ordered using each platform's default ranking system. The exact weighting of textual relevance, recency, engagement, uploader characteristics, geographic location, device or network information, and other ranking signals was not publicly available and could not be standardized across platforms. Creating new accounts reduced personalization based on prior viewing and search histories, but it could not eliminate cold-start recommendations, platform-specific ranking rules, temporal variation, geographic effects, or possible nondeterministic variation in search results. The retrieved videos should therefore be interpreted as a cross-sectional sample of highly visible results returned under the prespecified search conditions, rather than as a probability sample or exhaustive representation of all hepatitis B-related videos available on each platform. 2.3Data extraction and classificationThe following information was extracted for each video on the search date: platform, video URL, uploader identity, number of likes, collections, comments, and shares, uploader follower count, video duration, upload date, and days since upload. Likes, collections, comments, and shares were defined as user engagement indicators. Follower count was treated as an uploader-level characteristic, whereas video duration and days since upload were treated as structural video characteristics. The platform-specific save or favorite function was harmonized as “collections” for cross-platform analysis. All engagement data were recorded on the same date to reduce variation caused by the continuous accumulation of user interactions.Uploader identity was classified into four mutually exclusive categories according to the account profile, platform verification information, and stated institutional affiliation:Medical personnel: individual accounts identified as physicians, nurses, pharmacists, or other licensed or verifiable healthcare professionals;Normal users: individual accounts without a verifiable healthcare professional identity or official medical institutional affiliation, including patients, caregivers, and members of the general public;Medical institutions: official accounts operated by hospitals, clinics, public health institutions, or other healthcare facilities; andOther organizations: accounts operated by nonmedical organizations, media organizations, nonprofit organizations, social organizations, or commercial enterprises.When uploader identity was unclear, the account profile and platform verification information were jointly reviewed by the two evaluators, and disagreements were resolved through discussion with the senior evaluator.Video content was coded using five non-mutually exclusive topic categories:Symptoms: clinical manifestations, signs, or symptoms associated with HBV infection;Causes: HBV etiology, transmission routes, risk factors, and mechanisms of infection;Prevention: vaccination, screening, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, infection-control measu…

title: Semi-quantitative ultrasound scoring reveals hepatic structural recovery and immune modulation during tenofovir alafenamide therapy in chronic hepatitis B
abstract: Objective This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic response to tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF) in chronic hepatitis B (CHB) using a semi-quantitative ultrasound (US) scoring system, and to investigate the correlation between sonographic changes and immune function restoration. Methods A total of 100 CHB patients who received TAF monotherapy (25 mg/day) for at least 24 months were retrospectively enrolled. A seven-parameter semi-quantitative US score, encompassing liver echogenicity, capsular contour, margin shape, vessel clarity, portal vein diameter (PVD), spleen thickness (ST), and splenic vein velocity (SVV), was calculated at baseline, 12 months, and 24 months. Concurrently, serum hepatitis B virus (HBV) deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), peripheral T-cell subsets, including cluster of differentiation 3-positive (CD3 + ), CD4 + , CD8 + T cells, CD4+/CD8+ ratio, and natural killer (NK) cell activity were measured. Correlations between US scores and biochemical/immune parameters were analyzed. Results At 24 months, all patients achieved HBV DNA <20 IU/mL, with ALT and AST normalization rates of 92% and 95%, respectively. The comprehensive US score decreased significantly from 7.86 ± 1.73 at baseline to 3.37 ± 0.95 at 24 months ( P < 0.001), with the most pronounced improvements observed in capsular smoothness and parenchymal homogeneity. The CD4 + T-cell proportion and CD4 + /CD8 + ratio increased, whereas the CD8 + proportion decreased; NK cell activity rose from 42.7 ± 7.3% to 52.4 ± 6.2% ( P < 0.05). The US score was positively correlated with ALT (r = 0.56) and AST (r = 0.47), and negatively correlated with the CD4 + /CD8 + ratio (r = −0.46) and NK cell activity (r = −0.38) (all P < 0.01). Conclusion These findings indicate that TAF not only suppresses viral replication and normalises liver enzymes but also promotes measurable structural liver improvement, as reflected by declining semi-quantitative US scores. The strong correlations of US scores with biochemical and immune parameters support its utility as a non-invasive imaging biomarker for monitoring treatment efficacy and hepatic repair.
